Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate on the second reading of Bill C-183 briefly and for the purpose of dealing with but one aspect of the legislation. In doing so I shall be reciting a bit of history, and I do so not just because of the interest I have in the story to which I should like to refer but because I think there are one or two points about one change being made to the Canada Labour Code concerning which there should be clarification from the government side.
When I first came to parliament back in 1942, there were still living a large number of employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway who had lost their pension rights as a result of the 1919 general strike in the city of Winnipeg. speechtext:
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, my predecessor as the member for the constituency of Winnipeg North Centre, the late J. S. Woodsworth, during the years that he was in parliament did his very best to persuade the government to take the necessary steps to restore the pension rights that were lost by those CPR workers. I would point out that employees of other organizations, such as Canadian National Railways, the Manitoba government telephones and certain other groups, who lost their pension rights at the time of the 1919 strike had those rights reinstated, but this was never done for the CPR employees.
When it became my privilege to succeed Mr. Woodsworth, one of the battles that I carried on was the attempt to get those rights reinstated. As a matter of fact, it took only a few more years until most of those who had lost their rights had passed on, so it soon became an issue no longer of concern to living people. However, the grievance that had been suffered was so serious that some of us felt legislation should be enacted to make sure that this kind of thing would not happen again.
Accordingly, in the middle forties I started using the device of private member's hour to present various bills in an effort to do this very thing, namely to protect pension rights against loss as a result of a strike or a lockout. My efforts in private members' hour in those days succeeded just as well as similar efforts in private members' hour succeed today. In other words, our proposals were talked out with kindness and approval.
In 1948, the then Minister of Labour, the Hon. Humphrey Mitchell, introduced the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. This, indeed, is the piece of legislation which, under the revision of the statutes in 1970, became Part V of the Canada Labour Code and, of course, it is Part V of the Labour Code which is being replaced by Bill C-183, now before us.
Accordingly, when the late Humphrey Mitchell brought in the bill to provide for the regulation of labour matters in 1948, I then started trying to move the appropriate amendment to that bill. The bill was referred to the appropriate standing committee, and in that standing committee I moved an amendment which would have had the effect of protecting pension rights against loss resulting from a strike. I regret to say that in the committee we lost. However, there are times when one does not give up, and when that bill came back to the committee of the whole house I tried once again to move an amendment. This time, in addition to such efforts as I made on the floor of
Canada Labour Code
the House, I consulted certain people behind the curtains, in their offices and so on, and did all I could to persuade people in high places that the request I was making was a reasonable and legitimate request that ought to be enacted into law.
As a matter of fact, one of the persons I approached was the Prime Minister of the day, the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King. I pointed out that during his years as Prime Minister he had in fact taken care of a number of grievances that arose during the 1910 labour disputes and the 1919 strike in Winnipeg. He finally expressed agreement that what I was requesting should be made part of the law of the land. Therefore, on June 17, 1948, in committee of the whole, when I moved my amendment that would protect pension rights against loss resulting from strikes, I was met, and I knew by this time this was going to happen, with a counter suggestion made by Mr. Chevri-er, who was then Minister of Transport, to the effect that my idea was acceptable, but that the government would like to spell it out in a few more words so it would be clear beyond any doubt.
Actually, the amendment I moved, and this is found at page 5369 of Hansard for June 17, 1948, was as follows:
That section 4, subsection 2(b) be amended by changing the period after the word "Act" to a comma, and adding thereafter the following words:
and without restricting the generality of the foregoing, no employer shall deny to any employee any pension rights or benefits to which he would otherwise be entitled by reason only of his ceasing to work as the result of a lockout or strike or by reason only of dismissal contrary to this act.
The reason those last few words about dismissal contrary to this act were inserted was that these words were already there in the subclause I was seeking to amend. The pages of Hansard for that day are in themselves interesting, although they do not tell the entire story. In any case, in the middle of that afternoon a point was reached when the then Minister of Transport, the Hon. Lionel Chevrier, got up and suggested that an alternative wording would be acceptable, and that wording was as follows, and I quote from page 5390 of Hansard for that day:
That section 4, subsection 2(b) be further amended by changing the period after the word "act" to a comma, and adding thereafter the following words:
"and without restricting the generality of the foregoing, no employer shall deny to any employee any pension rights or benefits to which he would otherwise be entitled by reason only of his ceasing to work after the commencement of this act as the result of a lockout or while taking part in a concerted stoppage of work due to a labour dispute where such lockout or stoppage of work has been enforced by the employer or called by the recognized representative of such employee, as the case may be, after all steps provided or contemplated by law have been taken through negotiation, collective bargaining, conciliation and arbitration to settle such dispute or by reason only of dismissal contrary to this act."
In other words, my simple wording was enlarged upon to make it crystal clear that the protection of pension rights against loss resulting from a strike or lockout was to apply only in the case of a clearly legal strike and, of course, it was to apply only after this act of 1948 came into force.
At the page to which I have referred, page 5390 of Hansard for June 17, 1948, it will be noted that I accepted

the alternative wording proposed by Mr. Chevrier, whereupon my amendment was withdrawn, Mr. Chevri-er's amendment was put and it was carried. At the next page, 5391, there is an indication that the bill was reported, read a third time and passed. In other words, Mr. Speaker, we won the battle and had a provision written into the federal legislation of this country that from then on workers were not to lose their pension rights only because they took part in a strike or were involved in a lockout, provided in the case of a strike that it was legal in terms of the legislation we passed at that time. The provision we thus won on June 17, 1948, was clearly written into the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, and the language I have quoted became part of section 4 of that act. Those words are to be found in subsection (2) of section 4.1 need not read the words again because I have already placed them on the record.
My point is that since 1948, the law has been crystal clear that what happened in 1919 cannot happen again; that pension rights are protected against loss resulting from a strike. I may say that within a very few years after that legislation was enacted by this parliament, most of the provincial legislatures copied those very words and put that language into their provincial labour laws. I know in this day and age it may seem unnecessary to think of requiring this kind of protection, but experiences in the early part of this century were very tragic and, as I say, this was an important gain to labour, to have this protection put into the law.

I was saying before the question was put to me, that one of the beneficial results of getting this kind of legislation into federal law was that most of the provinces adopted it, so it is not now possible for workers in Canada to lose their pension rights because of involvement in a strike.
I want to point out also that when the Statutes of Canada were revised in 1970, this provision was carried forward into Part V of the Labour Code which is chapter L-l of the Revised Statutes of 1970. Although there was a little rearranging of the words, the same idea is there and the provision is well set down in section 110 of Chapter L-I of Revised Statutes of Canada 1970. So far no change; so far, all is well. Now, as the parliamentary secretary pointed out, this provision does seem to be carried forward in the bill now before us, Bill C-183. He identified the clause, namely clause 184, of the bill now before us. The clause is under the general heading "Unfair Practices". At page 55 of the bill one can read at the top of the page:

No employer and no person acting on behalf of an employer shall.. .
Then, we drop to the bottom of the page and find the following in (d):
. .. deny to any employee any pension rights or benefits to which the employee would be entitled but for
(i)	the cessation of work by the employee as the result of a lockout or strike that is not prohibited by this Part, or
(ii)	the dismissal of the employee contrary to this Part;
Despite my suspicions being aroused when I see the
Liberals making a change, I have read that clause backwards and forwards a dozen times and I think it is all right. There are now only about as many words in that clause as there were in the amendment I moved back in 1948. The Liberals of that day multiplied the number of words about four times. One reason I have entered this debate is that I understand the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) wants to assume his right to close the debate at the end of second reading and I hope he will give us the assurance that the shortening and changing of the language does not detract by one iota from the basic principle, namely, that pension rights cannot be interfered with in any way because of a strike so long as it is a strike that is legal under the provisions of Part V of the Labour Code.
As I say, I have read the language proposed in 1948 that was in the former statute and that is in the Revised Statutes of Canada for 1970, and I have now read the wording in the new bill, but I would like from the minister the assurance that nothing has been lost by the change of the language or by the shortening of the sentence. I am sure he agrees with me, and I am sure this is what he wants, but I think it would be useful to have his clear statement that it is the intention of the government to continue to have in our law the reform which was won in 1948, namely, that pension rights cannot be lost or interfered with because of a strike.
However, one other change has taken place. If my good friend the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Perrault) will continue to follow the legislation that is before us I would ask him to take note of this: The Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act of 1948, in addition to section 4 which provides that pension rights cannot be interfered with because of a strike, contains a section under the heading "Enforcement", section 40, which reads:
Every person, trade union and employers' organization who violates section four or section five of this Act...
And Section 4 is the one which dealt with pension rights.
... is guilty of an offence and liable upon summary conviction,
(a)	if an individual, to a fine not exceeding one hundred dollars;
or

fine not exceeding one thousand dollars.
In other words, the Act of 1948 not only provided that pension rights could not be interfered with but also contained a declaration that any employer who did this was guilty of an offence which, on summary conviction, was subject to a fine. That provision for fines, and for treating

the offence as one subject to summary conviction, was carried forward in the Revised Statutes of Canada for 1970. For example, I read section 146 of Chapter L-I, which is the Canada Labour Code:

As I say, there was no change from the act of 1948 in the revision made in 1970. But now, when we pick up Bill C-183, the one we are dealing with today, I find there has been a change. May I at the risk of repeating myself make it clear that in the two previous versions to violate that section about pension rights put an employer in the position of being subject to summary conviction and a fine. But under Bill C-183 this seems to have been changed.
I see under the heading "Offences and Penalties" in clause 191 at page 62 of the bill two sub-clauses and it is the second one which is relevant. I shall read clause 191(2):
Subject to section 190 . . .
That does not do anything because it talks about strikes and lockouts.
.. . every employer or trade union who violates or fails to comply with any provision of this Part other than section 148, 184 or 185 is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding ten thousand dollars.
This is the very striking change to which I call attention. In the case of the act of 1948 and in the case of the Revised Statutes of 1970, it is clearly stated that to violate the section which deals with pension rights is an offence for which there can be a charge and, on summary conviction, a fine. But in the new bill it is clearly stated that clause 184, the clause having to do with pension rights, is excluded from the possibility of being treated as an offence and hence subject to the fines provided.
In my opinion the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration is the kind of lawyer I am. You know, we pick up our knowledge of law around here. There may be other lawyers who can explain this to me. My hunch, from having listened to explanations around this place, is that the change probably would result in a person who suffered any wrong having a civil action because some law had been broken, but what has been taken away is the making of this unlawful act an offence subject to summary conviction. I feel very strongly that this lighter treatment in this kind of provision should not remain as it is. I say again I welcome the fact that the provision we won in 1948 has been carried forward. Try as I can, I cannot see anything wrong with the new wording. I think the protection is just as good in the shorter wording as in the 1948 longer version, but I am disappointed and disturbed over the fact that it was previously an offence for an employer to interfere with pension rights because of involvement in a strike, whereas this bill removes that offence. In that sense, there is that much less
Canada Labour Code
protection for the worker involved. I hope that when the Minister of Labour responds at the end of this debate, he will deal with this phase of the matter.
As I said, I rose to take part in this debate to deal just with this one matter. My colleagues have spoken generally on Bill C-183. We in this party welcome this bill. The only substantial change we would like to see would be the one that has been asked for, namely that current contracts should be renegotiable with respect to the technological change provisions. But generally speaking, we like the legislation and we hope that it will soon reach the statute books. However, I appeal to the minister when he responds at the end of this debate to do two things for me; one, to give me the assurance that the shorter wording of the provision protecting pension rights is just as meaningful as the longer version was and, second, to assure me that consideration will be given to keeping it as it was, namely, that interference with pension rights because of involvement with a strike is an offence that should be dealt with severely. We do not want any more incidents which cause suffering of the type which occurred in 1910 and 1919. I remind the minister that the provinces copied the earlier legislation, and if we weaken it in any respect at the federal level, they are likely to weaken it too.
I thank the minister for his attention to this one issue which I regard as very important.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-183 is obviously put forward by the government at this time in an attempt to solve the dilemma in which Canada finds itself as a nation which is highly dependent upon trade for its economic survival. When one considers that this country exports about 30 per cent to 40 per cent of its gross national product, and when one considers that those goods are going into markets where the competition is very severe, one realizes that there must be technological advancement in order to enable producers to compete effectively in these world markets. Competition is essential if we are to maintain the standard of living to which we have become accustomed, and if we are to maintain employment at the desired level in Canada. On the other hand, it is also obvious that as new technology is introduced into industry, whether it be by way of materials or by way of machines, the human factor will be involved increasingly. Men or women are necessarily laid off, sometimes in large numbers, in order to accommodate these technological advances or changes.
This bill, as I see it, is an attempt to solve this problem to get us off the horns of this dilemma. At the outset, I would like to say that in principle I agree wholeheartedly with this bill. When I wrote to the former minister of labour some time ago, I said, among other things, that I supported completely the basic principle underlying the Freedman report, namely, that we should not plunge blindly ahead seeking quantitative changes at the expense of human dignity. I firmly believe we must take steps to ensure that the security of people who are disadvantageously affected by the introduction of technologically innovative devices is protected, and that such people are given the opportunity to adapt to changed conditions and to participate in a meaningful way in Canadian society.

Despite that feeling, I do think that the bill with which we are dealing here must be looked at more closely in committee. In the first place, this bill applies only to members of organized unions. It does not apply to all members of the labour force over which the federal government has jurisdiction. Everyone probably knows that there are in excess of 500,000 people within federal jurisdiction governed by the provisions of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, but only half of those belong to trade unions. It would be nice if some sort of minimum standard could be established in this bill or in another bill, which would provide the same type or protection to those members of the work force who are not members of organized unions but who nevertheless may just as easily be affected by the introduction of technological advances by their employers. I know it may be difficult, but I think it is something that the committee should study well and on which possibly it could make recommendations.
There is one other point which is most deserving of study. Under the bill as it is presently constituted, a bone fide union bargaining in good faith and a bona fide company bargaining in good faith may enter into a collective agreement which will provide the machinery for settling problems which might occur as a result of the introduction of technological change in that particular industry. In other words, the union and the company will sit down and negotiate their contract provisions, either spelling out what will be done in the event that a number of employees are displaced or providing the machinery for settling any disputes which might arise in the event of such an occurrence. In all of these cases, those agreements will provide that in the event of disputes between the bargaining agents, the union and the company, the disputes will be handled by way of grievance procedure. If these disputes are not settled by the use of the grievance procedure, they will end up in front of the board of arbitration-whose decision will be binding on all parties. This will be the result if bona fide unions bargain in good faith with bona fide companies who also bargain in good faith.
On the other hand, if a union does not so bargain or if a company does not so bargain with the result that the agreement which is reached between them does not contain any provision which would take care of people who might be displaced in the event of technological change, under the provisions of this act the union would have the right to apply to the Canada Labour Relations Board which would have the power to grant to that union the right to bargain, and eventually even to strike. So, we have this contradiction. The bona fide union and the bona fide company which bargain in the spirit which we all want, end up with an agreement which could lead to binding arbitration in the event of a dispute. On the other hand, those unions or those companies which do not bargain in the way we wish would end up in a situation in which the union really has more power potentially because it can be given the right to strike in the event of disputes arising as a result of the displacement of people resulting from the introduction of technological change.
It seems to me that this is an anomaly which must be corrected, because I do not feel that the bona fide union and the bona fide company should be put in a weaker position or a position which they might find less acceptable than that of a union which, possibly for many rea-

sons, does not wish to bargain on this very important point. We must remember that despite the provisions of this particular bill, especially those dealing with technological change, unions now have the power to bargain on these very points. I, for one, would like to see less governmental interference in this area. I am a firm believer in free collective bargaining, and the freer it is the better. However, I also realize that not all companies are perfect, and not all unions are perfect.
Since each group is composed of human beings, the representatives of companies and unions on occasion tend to display the human frailties which we all possess. As a result, I have come to the conclusion that there should be some governmental intrusion in this area. There should be some incentive given to unions and companies to bargain in this very important area. However, if the bill remains as presently worded, I cannot see how a union would be given any incentive to bargain. If a union knows that if it does not bargain it may end up with the right to strike in the event of a dispute, why should it bargain and end up with nothing better than the right to submit to binding arbitration?
I suggest a compromise, Mr. Speaker. I know it has been suggested before, but I do not think it has been suggested in this context. It is that those companies which we seek to cover under this clause of the bill should be given no more than the unions and companies which bargain in good faith. In other words, we should consider the concept of introducing some type of compulsory arbitration in the event that disputes arise should technological change be introduced and, as a result, a significant number of employees are displaced.
There is one further point I would like to touch on with reference to this bill. It concerns the clause dealing with the inclusion of supervisory personnel in bargaining units. What exactly is meant by this clause is not too clearly spelled out. I hope the committee will examine it closely. I suspect that what is meant is supervisory personnel at the lowest level. If that is the case, a problem arises because it is the supervisory personnel at the lowest level who, so to speak, are given the job of enforcing the rights of the company under a collective agreement.
It is the lower level supervisory people who have the day to day job of meeting with union stewards and members of a union on the job, and who deal with disciplinary matters. It might well be that they could be included in the same bargaining unit, but I wonder what would be the position of an individual if he were asked to discipline one of his own union members, one of his union brethren. His would be a very difficult situation. I do not think he could wear two hats. This provision opens up the possibility of innumerable situations involving conflict of interest. It is something that has not been much discussed one way or the other. I hope the committee will look into this provision closely, to make sure we are not setting up an arrangement under which there will be such a conflict of interest at a very basic level in any plant.
Having made these few remarks, Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend the government for the attention it paid to submissions which were made, not only to the present

minister but to the previous minister, after the original bill was introduced. The changes that have been made during the last few months have cleared up a number of problems that existed previously. I hope the presem minister keeps an equally open mind during the committee discussions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want very much to take part in this debate not because I am an expert on labour legislation but because, like most citizens of Canada, I am very much concerned at the labour picture which appears in our country today. At the outset, I wish to commend my colleagues, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand (Mr. Knowles), on the stand they have taken in this debate because I believe they reflected the thinking of the majority in our party. They realized, in a sympathetic and sensitive way, that today labour has a major problem.
These hon. members agree with me that the growing confrontation between labour and the management of corporate structures has an ever increasingly serious effect on the whole population of Canada, and not just on those portions of the population directly affected by particular disputes. One thing we tend to forget is that we are dealing with legislation affecting the main trade unions in Canada. I point out that there are a tremendous number of Canadian workers who are not tied into labour unions. Unfortunately, or possibly fortunately, the tremendous ramifications of government legislation also affect these workers seriously.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Edmonton West, this occasion gives the government a rare opportunity to see if this legislation can be improved in committee, improved so as to provide leadership for the country and for the provinces concerning a problem that has assumed tremendous proportions within the last few years. More and more, the government is being asked by organized labour and the corporate structure of industry to introduce legislation that will strengthen their respective stands, not only in disputes now under way but in the settlement of disputes that may occur in the future.
Through a process of natural evolution, unions and other organized groups of labour have begun banding .together in order to present a stronger front. This has caused the banding together of industries in order to present equally strong opposition. This polarization has gradually brought the country into a position in which many Canadians suffer greatly when an industrial dispute or strike takes place. I do not think the harmful effects which follow strikes are intended, but are spinoffs because of the nature of the action taken. I point to some recent results of such actions in a dispute between employer and employee of which you are well aware, Mr. Speaker. Not long ago an entire city was paralyzed by a fall of snow and a strike of snow removal crews. I will not go into the issue of whether these employees were right or wrong, but a tremendous catastrophe could have come about had there been an outbreak of fire or lawlessness because there was no way in which the population of that city could have been protected.
Canada Labour Code
We are finding that the power of labour has continually increased in this evolution to the extent that it is now possible for very small groups in the labour force to walk out and, because they are affiliated with a larger group, to ensure that their picket lines will not be crossed. In this way a very few people can bring severe hardship to the majority of the citizens of Canada. This is only one of the problems we must look at today.
The second problem that has been brought out by all members who have spoken has been that very often a dispute between a trade union and industry causes a breakdown in normal production so that contracts are lost as well as productivity which sometimes are never recovered. It is Canada as a whole, not just the trade unions or industry, that suffers very dramatically in these circumstances. One unfortunate circumstance which results from a prolonged strike is that many small corporations and individual businesses go into bankruptcy. The strike makes it impossible for them to carry on normal business, so, they are forced to discontinue their operation.
These are the problems to which we should direct our attention, the problems which face all Canadians, and they must be solved. This is why, with my colleagues, I look forward to this legislation going to the committee where I am sure very serious consideration will be given to it. I hope that the government will be ready and willing to accept amendments from whichever party they come. The whole problem must be attacked by parliament, Mr. Speaker.
An ugly situation is developing in Canada today. People who are not affected by the financial outcome of a strike are becoming disillusioned with the use of the strike to settle major problems. All across the North American continent there is the realization that, although strikes were necessary to ensure labour a satisfactory return for its efforts in past years, they may have reached the end of their usefulness as a tool. But, Mr. Speaker, we cannot demand that trade unions give up this tool which, after all, is the only major implement they have to obtain what they feel are their just deserts. In all fairness, I do not believe that we can ask them to forgo this right unless we, as representatives of the people, can offer a substitute that is logical and plausible and which will achieve this end.
Perhaps the labour legislation in the United States which provides for a cooling-off period is a start. Labour unions quickly found that they needed legal expertise to survive, and today they employ some of the best legal brains available. The same can be said for the corporation; their legal officers are experts. At the federal and provincial level, there are in the departments of labour men who have dealt with the problem for years and through study and observation have learned a tremendous amount about the problems involved. Surely, it would be possible for the government to take the initiative to get these three groups together to see if the problem can be solved. I am not in any way suggesting that this has not been attempted, but unfortunately most of the effort has been directed toward solving a particular strike

April 18, 1972
Canada Labour Code
rather than to achieve the long range solution that is so necessary.
The government has a tremendous responsibility with regard to this legislation, Mr. Speaker. We in the official opposition, and I think I speak for the majority of our members, hope that this is not just another exercise to put up-to-date legislation on the books, but is rather an honest effort on the part of the government to provide a vehicle that can be used to prevent some of the problems we have encountered in the last three or four years. I think there is no question in the mind of any member of this House but that we are embarked upon a collision course between the trade unions and the corporate structure of this country. Every time there is a confrontation between these two there is no winner. Trade union representatives never achieve all they feel they should have. Industry always feels that it has granted more than it should have granted.
So, looking at it practically, when an agreement is reached and a contract signed, both sides to the dispute are granted time in which to prepare for the next confrontation. These agreements never solve anything. By buying time, both sides are able to prepare immediately for the next round of confrontation, which they each know will take place. Thus we see a polarization taking place between the great colossus representing labour and the great colossus representing industry and management, with labour making ever more demands, the confrontations becoming ever more severe, and ever more Canadians being involved and being hurt. That is why I plead today for the government to make full use of this opportunity and, in committee, not to try to process this bill quickly. Let us consider it honestly and sincerely. Let there be consultation between all parties in this House and those who will be most affected. Let us try to bring in legislation that will begin solving some of these major problems.
The kingpin on which this legislation turns is whether or not technological changes are sufficient grounds for the reopening of a contract once it has been entered into by both parties. This is of vital importance to both sides. As I say, we are dealing with two giants, and not with two individual organizations. Naturally, trade unionists are greatly concerned about whether technological changes mean a loss of jobs. They have learned from experience that most technological changes, either temporary or permanently, lead to loss of jobs. On the other hand, industry says that without technological changes it cannot streamline its enterprises and compete in international markets. These are fixed positions. The issue this bill raises is simply this: is technological change, when introduced during the life of a contract, basis enough for renegotiating the entire contract? Labour says yes and management says no, so there is confrontation. It is in this area that parliament is responsible. We must bring in legislation which will make it possible for parliament to guide both sides, for the good of the citizens of Canada.
Most people in Canada are not thoroughly versed in the fine points of labour law or the fine points of contract settlement. They do not want to be so versed. What they do want is the type of Canada where, day after day, they can earn a living for their families. Most families under-
(Mr. Danforth.]
take expenditures or obligations which are paid slowly, on budget plans. Our people do not want their normal earning power interrupted by a strike that may not touch them directly but may affect them indirectly. Such a strike may curtail their opportunity for making a living, or their means of transport, or their means of communication. These are the things in which our people are interested. Think of the service we can render the people of Canada and the workers of the world if we, in this House, can formulate a reasonable way of settling these disputes and so avoid the violent confrontations which have been so costly. I think that is what we are trying to do.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak in the debate on Bill C-183, an act to amend the Canada Labour Code. I have listened with a great deal of interest to spokesmen from both sides of the House and have found that I agree with many of the views expressed. At the same time, I must point out that there are always two sides to every question. I have sometimes felt, over the years, that organized labour has received many black eyes which, frankly, I do not think it has deserved. Without doubt, sometimes criticism could be levied at certain strikes which have taken place. Quite frequently, however, the cause lies much deeper than the dispute itself. Setting proper conditions in the economy would, I believe, bring more benefit to the Canadian nation, especially if we could do so in a manner that would ensure that all groups of Canadian society, whether organized labour, pensioners, those in unions and those not in unions, could share in the increasing prosperity which we enjoy every year. So far we have not in Canada, unfortunately, devised a plan for sharing fairly among all Canadians our annually increasing prosperity which is reflected in terms of the gross national product. That is the end to which parliament and hon. members should be working in their attempt to find solutions for the labour-management problem which seems to be with us currently.
This is an interesting and important bill, Mr. Speaker. It contains some new provisions and some necessary changes to existing legislation. It is my intention to support it. I trust, however, that the minister will incorporate in the legislation some of the proposed changes offered by various hon. members in the debate. May I point out that inadequate legislation and lack of real understanding of labour problems on the part of government and manage-* ment has led to much labour unrest and to many unnecessary strikes over the years.
The present act governing federal jurisdiction in the labour field was introduced in 1948. A few amendments over the years were made to it; but there is no doubt that it has long been out of date and in need of major revision. That is why organized labour has generally indicated that the proposed legislation is an improvement over the old and should be endorsed, despite some of the rather weak clauses in the bill. Other members of my group have dealt with various aspects of the legislation, so I will not cover those aspects again at this time. It is my wish, however, to deal briefly with several interesting aspects of labour problems. I should like to make a few general comments first on the general labour situation in Canada.
April 18, 1972

A few weeks ago the Canadian Labour Congress and the Canadian Railway Labour Association made their annual submissions to the federal government. Both briefs called for a number of major changes in the government's economic policy and advocated changes which would greatly improve the living standards of all Canadians. Too few people in our country give credit to organized labour for the job it has done over the years to improve the lot of all Canadians, not merely those who belong to some particular labour union. Labour has led the fight to improve social conditions and living standards all over this nation and the improved lot of the average workingman is testimony to the success of its campaign.
I can recall the struggle of some of the early unions for better conditions. Mr. Speaker, I live in a mining area and I know of miners who were blacklisted in every mining camp for having had the courage to strike for such things as the 8-hour day and the 40-hour week. They were blacklisted for wanting clean sheets in the camps and improved safety conditions in the mines. Those of us who have followed them enjoyed the benefits they won for us, although at the time the general public had little sympathy for them. No one today would suggest that they were not justified in their fight for better conditions at that time. The same arguments were used against labour then as now, namely that industry could not afford to meet the cost, but somehow we have survived as a nation and the living standard of Canadians has improved.
An example of labour interest in the welfare of Canadians generally was shown in the briefs presented to the federal government by the CLC and the CRLA. They called for a number of major social improvements, including such things as the war against poverty, and advocated an all-out attack against the increase in poverty which we are experiencing in this country. The briefs called for a guaranteed annual income and an increase in the old age security pension to $100, payable at 60 years of age. They requested the government to establish a cost of living index which would indicate the actual increases in living costs. The briefs called for a revised policy on Unemployment Insurance which would exclude severance pay and vacation pay from the classification of earnings under the act. They requested that severance pay and vacation pay be looked upon as deferred wages or savings, which they are really.
The briefs of these labour unions dealt with pollution problems. Again they requested the federal government to bring in national standards and to enforce the regulations for the clean-up of our environment. They called for more research on environmental problems. The briefs dealt with tax reform, one of the major problems facing this nation. They requested that adequate tax legislation be introduced by this government and that a tax system be established which would bring equality to all Canadians. They urged the government to take action on housing and trade problems, as well as problems dealing with our native people. This is a clear indication that organized labour is interested in the whole Canadian scene, not only in their own union activities. I believe that this is sometimes overlooked by members of parliament and Canadians generally.
Canada Labour Code
I would like to make just one more point on this general position of labour in this and in other countries. The workman has only one thing to sell, his labour. In my opinion, he should have the right to organize and bargain collectively. This bill retains that right. I certainly endorse this aspect of the legislation which we are being asked to vote upon.
I would now like to get down to one or two points in the legislation. While I intend to endorse the bill when the vote comes, I still feel there are several sections which the minister should look into and, I hope, amend. One deals with a basic industry, fishing. I point out to the minister that for years fishermen have been fighting for the rights which any group of workers should have under the various labour jurisdictions in Canada. The present legislation will not give the same protection to fishermen that other labour groups will enjoy. In my opinion, all workers in the fishing industry are entitled to full protection under the Canada Labour Code. For this reason, the definition of a fisherman in this current bill must be changed. I understand that the present wording of the definition will exclude about 75 per cent of the fishermen. I urge the minister to check this very closely and bring in the necessary change to give this group of workers the protection they should have. I see no reason why any group of workers in Canada, regardless of the occupation they pursue, should be discriminated against.
An excellent brief was presented to members of parliament by the United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union some weeks ago. Points in this brief have already been raised by several of my colleagues and others, so I will not repeat them at this time. However, when this bill goes to committee, I urge the minister to invite representatives of this union to present their views. They should be closely questioned on their proposed amendments. I trust that something constructive will come out of this so that this group of workmen will have the coverage they should have under Canada's Labour Code.
There is another point I am going to raise. It is touched upon in the legislation. This deals with discrimination against workmen because of age. I recently had an example in my own area of a man 51 years of age who was denied employment because he was too old. I have taken up this case with the labour department and they are investigating it. This rank discrimination against workmen must stop. We must incorporate in legislation sufficient safeguards to make certain that people in this category are protected against discrimination in any industry in Canada. I am not certain that we have all the necessary safeguards. They certainly ought to be incorporated in a Labour Code because in our industrialized society, we are reaching the stage where industry is more interested in the younger workers than those who are getting on toward retirement age. This is another field where we will run into a great deal of trouble unless discrimination of this type is nipped in the bud. I feel it should be done through legislation.
There is another matter I would like to discuss briefly. I think this is one of the most important items in the whole field of labour-management relations. I am going to talk briefly about conciliation procedures. In my opinion, it is in this area that one of the major weaknesses in labour

April 18, 1972
Canada Labour Code
relations lies. I do not think we have enough skilled labour negotiators. I do not think that governments generally, federal or provincial, have paid sufficient attention to this very important aspect of settling a dispute between labour and management. Much more can be done. One of the worst examples in Canada of this weakness is our own federal government. Time after time, we find that negotiations do not begin until the expiry date of the contract is very close. Sometimes the expiry date of the contract passes before finally, in desperation at the lack of progress being made in the negotiations the workers are driven to strike. This should not be. This is part and parcel of the conciliation procedures which I think should be looked into and updated.
The federal government should be the employer in Canada that sets standards. It should be the employer in Canada that gives guidance to other employers in the treatment of agreements that become due. But in many instances we have seen the sorry spectacle of the federal government being one of the worst offenders as far as labour contracts are concerned. I trust that from now on we will see an improvement in this regard.
We have had a great deal of discussion about technological change, and to me this is the most important aspect of the whole bill. Our group welcomes the inclusion of provisions in the legislation dealing with technological change. There is no point in burying our heads in the sand, because technological change is with us and is increasing in scope. The mere fact that these provisions are included in the legislation is an indication that we are looking to the future.
There is no doubt that we are going to run into trouble in this regard. Workers in some industries are very apprehensive about their jobs and will try to protect them in negotiations with management. This is one other problem facing Canada today. If our economy guaranteed a job to every Canadian who wanted one, and I believe it is the right of every Canadian to have a job if he wishes to work, I am quite certain many of these strikes which currently take place would not arise. I think it is the failure, not only of the government but of the members of the House, to set up an economy that guarantees work for individuals that is often the basic cause of much of the labour-management unrest that we have in this country.
We hear a lot about the loss to the economy through strikes, and I frankly admit that this loss is very serious. But there are other losses that are much more serious. Take, for example, unemployment. There are some 650,000 Canadians who are out of work every day of the month. Over the course of one year, this means about 150 million working days are lost. In the case of workers who for reasons of ill health are forced to lay off work, the number of man days lost is far greater than the man days lost as a result of strikes. I am not trying to say that work days lost through strikes is not a serious matter because it is, and we should try to bring the parties together so that we can lessen the number of strikes taking place in this country. But surely we must look at the situation in perspective and realize that there are other areas in which the loss of work days is far more serious than the loss that is usually attributed to striking unionists.
[Mr. Harding.)
Again may I point out I am certain that the tightening up of our labour procedures will help materially to improve labour-management relations. This is the reason I am so pleased to see the progress that is apparently being made in the field of labour relations through the implementation of this legislation. I shall not say more, Mr. Speaker. When the bill comes back to the House, we shall have an opportunity of seeing any changes that have been made in the committee. Again, I urge the minister to look very carefully at the suggestions that have been made by various groups. I hope that when the bill returns to the House we will see a further tightening up of the legislation which I and most Canadians hope will bring about a better era of labour-management relations in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Martin P. O'Connell (Minister of Labour):
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS, LABOUR RELATIONS BOARD, INDUSTRIAL INQUIRY COMMISSIONS AND CONCILIATION BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. I want to thank all hon. members who have participated in the debate over the past several days for the contributions they have made. I particularly want to express my gratitude for the general climate of opinion evident from the contributions made by members on both sides, which I take to be an opinion favourable to the principles of the bill. I think this bodes well for the debate that we will be having at the committee stage.
Having listened to the members of various opposition parties and members on this side of the House, I feel that there has been a general endorsement of the basic principles of the bill, though some caution has been expressed. Interest has been shown in specific clauses, and during the committee stage we will have the opportunity of exploring these. I welcome the attendance of members at the committee stage and I assure all hon. members that, so far as the Minister of Labour is concerned, it will be very worthwhile to issue an invitation to any interested groups in the country to come forward and make representations.
I recognize that this bill has come forward at a time when there is very high public interest in labour disputes. Indeed, this interest is not only high but is coloured and sharpened with a certain degree of irritation. It comes at a time when there is a large amount of group militancy, not only in Canada but in many other countries as a result of efforts made to change social, economic and other conditions under which people live. Therefore, we find a bill which is the first attempt to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act in 24 years coming forward at a time when people are far more critical and less passive than they have ever been in the past. This is why I am encouraged to hear there is a general acceptance of the broad approach reflected in this bill through the endorsement of it by members on both sides of the House.
The bill in its broadest sense is designed to put a legal framework around the collective bargaining process and to regulate the relationships between employers and employees in the public interest. I trust that is what we
April 18, 1972

will conclude even when we have been through the committee stages and various members have brought forward their specific criticisms.
The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) expressed general support. He modified it with some caution and drew particular attention to the recommendation of the Woods task force concerning a public interests disputes commission. Other members have drawn attention to this proposal. I have studied it very carefully, and I have concluded it would not be a contribution to dispute settlement in Canada. I am not going to go into the reasons for that at this stage, but I know it will come forward in committee and I should like us to have a very thorough investigation of that proposal to see exactly what it would mean, particularly for us as parliamentarians. It has very serious implications for the role of government in dispute settlement, and particularly for the role of members of parliament. It will be a good thing to have that out in committee to see every side of it.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) highlighted the technological provisions in the bill, but seemed to be saying that employers should be in the same position whether or not they had provision or procedures to deal with technological change. I may have understood him wrongly, but as I listened I thought he was saying that even though there are provisions or procedures an employer ought to be put into the position of having a contract reopened during its closed season. We have not taken that approach, and because we have not there are exemptions from technological change provisions inserted in the bill. I hope that question, too, will come forward at the committee stage.
The hon. member for Gamelin (Mr. Portelance) made a very interesting contribution in drawing our attention to the New Zealand experience, which is also the experience in another Commonwealth country, Australia, where there are mandatory arbitration procedures and the use of labour courts. He indicated quite clearly that this process has its failures, that the mandatory or compulsory arbitration approach is not likely a successful one because there are strikes that just happen to be illegal. We have turned our backs on that process here in favour of a process that continues the Canadian experience of investigating disputes, going through a conciliation procedure with a mediation procedure following that.
When we look at the figures in respect of federal jurisdiction we have no reason for complacency, but we do have reason to believe it is a basically satisfactory procedure. About 95 per cent of the disputes into which the labour department has been drawn have been settled without strike action. Moreover, some very interesting statistics concerning man-days lost in the federal jurisdiction are available.
For example, in 1966 there were 133 man-days lost out of every 10,000 man-days worked. In 1971, that was down to 9 days lost out of every 10,000 days worked. We will not be able to maintain that level, undoubtedly, but I think it does reflect the building up of mediation procedures in the department under the former Minister of Labour. He is in the House this afternoon and I think we all want to
Canada Labour Code
welcome him back after his absence, just as we want to recognize the major contribution he has made to this bill I am now putting before the House. The mediation procedures launched during his time in office had a great deal to do with improving our experience in federal jurisdiction over the past three or four years.
The hon. member for Gamelin once again drew attention to the settlements on the St. Lawrence docks. I hope members will forgive me if I just allude to that again, but it, too, confirms and reinforces our confidence in the mediation procedure which goes into effect as soon as a contract is signed. It should be a constant and permanent feature as it is very helpful where there is a third party; an honest broker, a neutral observer or a person who gains the confidence of both parties to a dispute, works with them constantly and helps bring about an amendment to a contract during a period voluntarily agreed upon. This helps the parties calm down their emotional postures or positions that are adopted psychologically during these relationships, and this is very difficult to improve.
That mediation procedure was used in respect of the complex situation at the docks and the settlement that has emerged there is perhaps a milestone, as much as it is a monument to the previous Minister of Labour, in labour history. The wage settlement is extremely modest, but that is not the important thing at all. The important thing is that the employers, having combined in a council, looked at that situation; the longshoremen looked at their situation and the long-term future of the Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec docks, and came to the view that they could to the benefit of both sides exchange productivity, give up absolute work practices and gain real and effective productivity in exchange for job security and pension changes, and other things that have some real benefit.
As the hon. member for Gamelin mentioned, I think there are many other situations in Canada which can be described as technological laboratories where human relations are involved, where those involved could usefully follow the pattern which was instituted in respect of the docks, with particular relation to job security and the retirement benefits in exchange for the giving up of featherbedding practices and other work rules that really injure the Canadian economy as well as the economy of the local community.
In this bill we are seeking to encourage the parties to bring into their bargaining procedure the whole question of technological change. Many others here have referred to this as a basic element they want to support, regardless of other features of the bill about which they are not too sure at the present time.
All I want to say to the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) is that I appreciate the common sense he displayed. He ought to have stuck to his own remarks and omitted all those quotations, which really came from academics, many of which in my opinion were irrelevant to the situation and undermined the very common sense proposals the hon. member was making. He sounded better when he was on his own.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) reinforced his acceptance of the basic Freedman princi-

April 18, 1972
Canada Labour Code
pie, the right to bargain collectively in respect of the effects of technological change. I think he spoke for all of us in this regard. We all know that the labour force of Canada is not against technological change and does not want to retard or prevent it. Our whole future as an effective, modern economy depends on us absorbing that technological change and, in fact, putting it to work for us as a society. We do not want the effects of it to weigh so heavily and perversely on the employees of enterprise.
Many employers are approaching this matter in an intelligent way, recognizing a social and human responsibility, and we want to extend that principle, so far as we can, in the federal jurisdiction by encouraging the extension of this process. That is the basic feature of the bill.
The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Serre) represents an area with a very high organized labour population. I think he said that 80 per cent of his constituency is involved in the organized labour movement. I was encouraged to hear him say that this bill would not only be good for labour but would be good for management. I do not know that I will be able to comment on the very interesting remarks made by so many members on both sides of the House. I particularly wish to say I appreciated the remarks of the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne). He has a background in labour affairs as a result of his experience in the union movement, and he made a very useful contribution to the debate as it began on its first day. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) suggested the bill should encourage more of the sort of quiet process that was followed on the St. Lawrence docks. If he understood the bill, he would know that is exactly what it is trying to do. He suggested that the process that went on there is the very kind of thing that reduces the adversary approach. All of us know the kind of group militancy that is common in society, not only in the labour-management field. If we think about it for a moment we will see it as part of the social environment today.
We find as the complexity of society increases that the interdependence of all of us on each other increases and it becomes very difficult to effect change and therefore group militancy has become very common. We must contain that. We cannot turn it off entirely because we have a free society, but we must contain it. The kind of quiet activity which went on at the docks was exactly designed to contain it in the sort of framework we have created and are modifying now. What he was appealing for is exactly what we are trying to bring about in this bill.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked for certain assurances concerning clause 184 in the bill. I can give him the assurance that there is no intention to change the provisions respecting pensions, and in our view there has been no change in the protection of pension rights during or as a result of a strike. I think that was the assurance he wished. I want to say with as much clarity as I can that there was no intention to alter that which existed in the previous bill. In our view nothing has been altered from the previous bill with regard to those pension rights which might otherwise be affected by a strike.

Clause 191, subclause 2, omits the offence to which the hon. member referred going back to clause 184(3)(d). Now, may I refer him to clause 189. It is in that clause that we believe we have coped with it in even a better way by making it an unfair labour practice to be considered by the new Canada Labour Relations Board. In our view a fine may not be the right way in which to approach it. It is far more important to have the unfair labour practice brought before the Canada Labour Relations Board. The clause in question states that the Board may by order require the party to comply with that section and may do certain other things to enforce its order of compliance. We think perhaps the enforced compliance is better than a fine. Once again in the committee we would be glad to have opinions concerning whether we have done the better of two things. However, I do wish to give the assurance that there was no intention to retreat from the positions which existed previously.
I know there are many members who have raised very interesting points concerning arbitration procedures, concerning the supervisory personnel, concerning appointments to the Canadian Labour Relations Board and whether that board should be a representative board as we have understood the existing one to be or whether it should be a public interest board as we believe it ought to be. Interesting points were also raised concerning bargaining rights for professionals and other matters of that kind.
However, one other subject came up so frequently I want to refer to it specifically. It was brought up by the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour (Mr. Perrault), the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Mather), the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding). Many members have referred to the position of the fishermen. We have taken a step forward with regard to the bargaining rights of certain fishermen. It is true we have not covered all commercial fishermen. We do not want to leave the impression that there is discrimination. We have taken a step further with regard to those who share in the catch as fishermen. This provision is similar to the one which applies to dependent contractors in the trucking industry. We have grave concerns about going any further at this time. We have grave concerns over the legal question of the right of including others as employees under this act who may in fact not be employees. However, I did meet with the representatives of the Allied Fishermen's Council. I had a very good talk with them. I expressed a great deal of sympathy for the case they were making. I advised them we do not feel we can go further at this time than is being proposed but we will have it out again in the committee. So far as I am concerned, they are very welcome to return and I would appreciate it if they would
April 18, 1972

come back and place before the committee the case they are trying to make.
We know there are various provincial governments which are moving in this field, as in other fields, further than industry might like, as in the case of the pulpwood lot people who cut and sell pulpwood to others. There is a special question here and I want to express a great deal of sympathy in respect of the bargaining rights of these people concerning prices and other conditions. At the same time, however, I would of course be frank to say we may not have the jurisdiction and this question has to be settled.
Mr. Speaker, these remarks will conclude those I wish to make in closing this second reading debate. Let me again thank all those who participated. I believe they did so with a great deal of thought in this area and with a high spirit of interest. I look forward to meeting them again in the Standing Committee in the very near future. I hope we can get this bill into law so that its beneficial measures can become operative.
