speakeroldname: Mr. Robert C. Coates (Cumberland-Colchester North) moved
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING PUBLICATION OF RESULTS OF OPINION POLLS
speechtext:
that Bill C-15, to amend the Canada Elections Act (publication of the result of opinion polls) be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in speaking on Bill C-15, I would first like to place on the record the explanatory note that outlines the purpose of this bill. It reads as follows:
The purpose of this amendment is to prohibit, and to make punishable as an illegal practice, the publication in any manner before election day of the results of a poll of the political opinions of the electors. The proposed amendment does not prohibit the taking of such a poll for private purposes.
This is not the first time this bill has been debated in this chamber. Each time I have placed it on the order paper, I have found that it has produced a good deal of valuable discussion among the public and the media. I found that if it does nothing else, it at least makes the
Canada Elections Act
public aware of some of the dangers associated with opinion polls, especially those used during election campaigns and published by the media, particularly the newspapers of this nation. In my opinion, this practice all too often results in newspaper promotion stories about the polls rather than the merit of political parties' campaigns and the policies that are being proposed.
I first introduced the bill because of what happened in the last provincial election in the province of Quebec. I felt that newspapers used opinion polls to stampede the electorate to vote for the Liberal party of that particular province at that time because of issues that developed around the Parti Quebecois whose object was to separate Quebec from the remainder of Canada. In this regard, I would like to quote some comments that appeared in the press during that election campaign and one that followed in Great Britain which produced a similar result. These results indicate that most of the time opinion polls do more damage than they do good. All too often, the result of such publication is that people involve themselves in discussions about the relative strengths of political parties based on percentages reflected by these polls rather than the relevant strengths of political parties based on whether they have the policies that will be of greatest value to the future of either a province or the nation.
I should like to place on the record some of the comments made by Charles Lynch in an article that appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of May 7, 1970 concerning polls and what transpires when newspapers use them to try to convince the electorate that certain things may or may not happen. Mr. Lynch said in part:
The polls introduced a scare element into the campaign-
He is talking about polls that appeared in newspapers in the province of Quebec during the Quebec provincial election campaign.
-and had they not done so, there is reason to believe that the Parti Quebecois might have run up a larger vote on election day than was actually the case.
The polls led to the celebrated Brink's truck evacuation of Montreal.
Publication of the polls altered the tone of news coverage of the campaign, thrusting the separatist issue to the fore, and leading the CBC to decide that the election merited night-long, nationwide coverage on television.
It can be argued that the polls rendered a national service, if indeed they served to check the separatist surge and swing the undecided vote to the Liberal federalists-but however desirable the results, the fact remains that the polls intruded into the basic democratic process of holding an election.
The poll results became central to almost everything that was written about the Quebec election between April 18 and April 29. And they diluted what otherwise would have been the shock effect, provincial and national, of the size of the separatist vote on election night.
No political commentator is likely to argue for the abolition of advance polls, or straw votes as they used to be called, because they give us so much to write about in the course of a campaign.
They may even keep us from looking more foolish than we usually do, and for an example of that we need only look back to the British Columbia election last August.
Without the help of the polls, most commentators labored under the impression that the NDP would upset the government of Premier W. A. Bennett. When the results were in, the pundits headed for the border with the laughter of the victorious Mr. Bennett echoing in their ears.

April 18, 1972
1410____________________________________
Canada Elections Act
The voters had spoken, without benefit of opinion polls, which might or might not have influenced the result had they been legal.
People in my line of work realized how heavily we have come to depend on the polls in our campaign reporting, and we learned a badly-needed lesson about the importance of discussing election issues, rather than forecasting results.
The question is not whether or not the poll; are accurate-most of them are remarkably so. Rather, it's whether or not they distort the democratic process and, by depicting the voting pattern in advance, alter it.
It has been my contention that polls are and can be used for the particular benefit of the person or persons producing them. They can be accurate, as Mr. Lynch points out in his article, or they can be completely inaccurate. Their inaccuracy can do great damage by fooling people who do not usually pay much attention to newspapers but depend on them during election campaigns to provide them with the facts as seen by what they have come to believe are political analysts of some repute. Unless we have some type of regulation of opinion polls, they could be misused in a very dangerous manner.
I have pointed out in the past that there are two newspaper chains in this country to which such a large proportion of the reading public subscribes they can pump much information into their homes that may or may not be accurate. It is not good enough to say the people will find out eventually because, during an election campaign, people depend on the accuracy of what they are reading. If it is not accurate, it is too late after an election campaign to make corrections because decisions have been taken on the basis of what the people read. It is no help to say, what is the difference; what we said was inaccurate but has been corrected now.
I wish to give an example of another serious problem, that of the monopoly building up in the newspaper field. Although the figures may have increased now, some time ago Southam News Services had a readership of its various newspapers in Canada of 849,364. FP Publications had a readership across Canada of 858,589. So that between these two there are over 1.5 million readers. The Thomson chain had a readership of 371,006, though this figure may have increased now. This is an indication that the three combined have a readership of about two million daily.
If these newspapers were so inclined-I am not suggesting that they would be-they could join together to perpetuate the dissemination of a great deal of false information by means of polls, especially during the last week of an election campaign. This is why I am concerned at the lack of any regulation today. Any political party could publish a poll, and in such a way that the public would not know that the party concerned was putting out misinformation in order to create a certain impression in the minds of the voting public. This situation concerns not only me but, I am sure, many Canadians.
Many newspapers and individuals across this country are asking whether polls should or should not be allowed.
I believe there should be some kind of regulation that would at least ensure they had some authenticity; that there should be some requirement that must be met before they could promote whatever purpose the poll had [Mr. Coates.)
in mind. I do not know whether this will ever be the case but I do know that we should keep discussing the question if for nothing else than to make the public more aware that there is some doubt about the validity of polls and that they should not place too great a dependence upon them. If we are able to make people better aware that they should not read too much into polls or place too much dependence upon them, that polls can be inaccurate, then during the time that is available to us today we have at least accomplished something. As I see it, this is one of the values of private members' bills.
There will be a general election campaign not too long from now, whether in June, in October or next April or May. I would not like to see in the next general election in Canada a recurrence of what happened in Great Britain during the last general election campaign in that country. In that campaign the people of Great Britain were placed in the position where the political parties were not discussing anything but where they stood in the most recently published poll. They were concerned that the Labour party was ahead by six points, that the Conservative party was catching up and was behind by three points, and so on. Each newspaper had its own poll which it claimed was more accurate than any other. The pages of the newspapers which should have covered the policies being put forward by the two major political parties in that country were, instead, filled with information about what those newspapers were determining to be the public feeling as a result of the polls they were carrying out. This is an unfortunate situation and I should not like to see it repeated in this country during the next election campaign.
What we should see on the pages of newspapers during an election campaign are the issues in the campaign, the policies of the various political parties and views as to the best political party to suit the needs of the country. We should not be told that one political party has 45 per cent of the support of the electorate whereas another political party has only 38 per cent as a result of its present image. Rather, the people should be able to make an educated determination of which political party is best and should be given the responsibility of running the country for the next four or five years.
I should like to conclude my remarks by putting on the record some of the things Peter Dempson, who was an associate editor of the Toronto Telegram prior to its demise, had to say about opinion polls:
Should public opinion polls be banned in Canada prior to a general election?
After the fiasco of the polls in the recent British election, an increasing number of Canadians now believe they should be. Indeed, many people are convinced that political sampling before, and during, an election campaign can do more harm than good.
Their main cricicism is that professional pollsters often confuse, exaggerate, influence and even deceive the public when their findings are published.
That is my opinion, Mr. Speaker. I ask hon. members to support this bill.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING PUBLICATION OF RESULTS OF OPINION POLLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been interested by the remarks of the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates) in connection with a bill to amend the Canada Elections Act passed
April 18, 1972

in this House not more than eighteen months ago. Through his bill, the hon. member is simply seeking to prohibit the publication, before election day, of the results of public opinion polls conducted by various organizations in general or at election time.
This question was rather fully looked into when we considered the Elections Act, more particularly section 105, regarding what should or should not be published. The committee had concluded that to prohibit the publication of such results or polls would serve little purpose, mainly because we are living in a world of intercommunication, and that it would be extremely difficult to prevent any association from conducting polls and publishing the results in another country, and then from sending them back to this country at election time.
In my opinion, too much is made of such polls. In his comments, the hon. member suggested that they are aimed at altering election results.
On that point I cannot agree with him for the main reason that I think the Canadian electorate is a lot more mature when it comes to express its political opinion by vote or to be influenced by a poll.
The example given by the hon. member; namely the effect of a poll in the province of Quebec, with regard to the Parti Quebecois during the last provincial election is at least inaccurate. I think we can all recall clearly the case of a poll result that was clearly reversed by public opinion, therefore such a claim cannot be supported on the basis that the result of a poll may alter an elector's vote.
Can advance poll results influence a vote? I would think that they can perhaps to a certain degree, in view of the percentage of credibility given to them by public opinion, since the effect of those results is after all, to inform. But I have seldom seen people who could be influenced by them. On the contrary, as most hon. members, I have seen poll results being in favour of a political party which, on the basis of those results stopped working while its opponents kept up their effort and succeeded in reversing the poll results or in showing that they were false.
I spoke a while ago of what I consider in a way a serious lack of confidence in the maturity of the Canadian electorate if we want the agencies specializing in gallup polls for now on to stop publishing incomplete although very detailed results.
Such results, in my opinion, are meant to inform provided they carry some credibility. If they inform the population as a whole, they may have a beneficial influence on public opinion.
We must realize that during an election campaign, even though our communications are excellent, it can still be interesting and important, strictly from the point of view of information, to know what may be happening in other parts of the country.
But I doubt that this could really change the opinion of the elector. I think the Canada Elections Act, which the mover of this bill intends to amend, cannot go so far in forbidding the outflow of information.
Canada Elections Act
To my mind, publishing the results of a poll is giving out information. A while ago, my colleague mentioned that English newspapers were full of poll results which did not take into account the real political problems. I feel that instead of blaming the organizations which publish these results, he should blame the newspapers and the reporters for their lack of maturity in not giving the electors the required information.
I seriously believe that even if we wish to ensure in some way the secrecy of the vote and to avoid any external influence on the electors, we have just the same to provide him with valid information.
Since those media are now world wide, to forbid under a legislation the publication of polls would give more weight and significance to those polls whose results would anyway appear in foreign publications and would eventually be otherwise communicated. It would be extremely difficult, due to our various media, to prevent the people from getting acquainted with them.
The only thing to do is to explain the results of the polls to the people. In my opinion, the public have already shown that they are not taken by those results, that they accept them as valid information, and the tactics of men as well as politics are such that the political party which seems to be the favourite following a public poll tries to take advantage of it. Obviously! On the other hand, the party which may believe to have been wronged, strives harder to change public opinion.
One can mention the rather striking example of the forecast based on a Gallup poll showing that 3, 4, or 5 per cent of the Canadian voters would vote, for instance, for the Social Credit party at the next general election. In my opinion, no one would be surprised by such a forecast, neither would the Canadian voters as a whole be affected by it. Actually, I think that it would be a mere indication of the general trends, whereas anyone would still be at liberty to try and change public opinion.
I may add that even though the intent may be commendable, I cannot see really how any amendment to clause 105 of the Canada Elections Act, for instance, would entail the elimination of this type of forecasts, which by the way are given far more importance than they actually deserve. In other words, if these Gallup polls are of an informative nature, then I think that the information they supply is worthwhile and should be allowed publication.
I have faith at least more than the sponsor of this bill, in the sound maturity and the discriminating judgment of the Canadian people in regard to information. I do not, therefore, consider the information provided by Gallup polls more important than it actually is.
I fail to see in these circumstances how the proposed amendment to the Canada Elections Act can be effective and, above all, how we could put a stop to this kind of Gallup polls.
In conclusion, I must say that thanks to its maturity the Canadian people are in a position to cope with the problems raised by these Gallup polls or by any abusive interpretation of their findings.

April 18, 1972
Canada Elections Act

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that the hon. member for Cumberland-Col-chester North (Mr. Coates) has had the opportunity of introducing this bill. It is very timely in view of the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will likely call an election within the next couple of weeks. Whether or not we will be faced with an election very shortly depends to some extent on the result of polls now being conducted. I am very interested in this matter and have a bill on the order paper similar to the bill of the hon. member. I have no objection to the taking of polls but I object to the results being published during an election campaign.
A poll taken recently may have some bearing on whether the Prime Minister will call an election soon. It was conducted by the Gallup poll organization and showed that approximately 40 per cent of the Canadian public was unable to say how it would vote if an election were held immediately. I suppose the result of that poll scares the pants off the government, just as it would if the figure applied to the opposition. This might mean that the Canada First party with some effort would be able to pick up that 40 per cent and form a government. I suppose this means the Prime Minister has been hedging his bets for the last two or three weeks.
We all know that very little is being done in the way of legislation and very little is on the order paper to be done. We are waiting for the completion of a poll being conducted by the Liberals the results of which will, hopefully, indicate to the Prime Minister whether or not to call an election. This in itself is an indication that polls do have some influence on election procedures.
I understand the Conservatives have conducted recently at least three polls with varying successful results, depending upon how you view them. There is a portion of the Canadian public conditioned to reading ads published by soap companies, automobile companies and other entrepreneurs of the nation, many of which suggest that their product is the best. They might say that their product will get a person's teeth whiter than any other toothpaste. They say they have conducted a survey which shows that 99 per cent of the school children who were asked indicated that Crest is the best toothpaste. Another one will say that Close-up ensures the whitest teeth and also freshens your breath. Another poll will indicate that Ultra Brite, to the extent of 99 per cent, has been proven to be the most successful whitener of one's teeth. A large number of people in our nation believe that one must be on the winning side and therefore must use Listerine although it tastes very bad, because tests and surveys have proven it to be the best.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING PUBLICATION OF RESULTS OF OPINION POLLS
speechtext: What about Scope?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT CONCERNING PUBLICATION OF RESULTS OF OPINION POLLS
speechtext:
Exactly the same claims are made for Scope. This, of course, is where the problem arises. It depends upon who takes the survey and the purpose for which it is taken.
Recently I prepared a questionnaire for the people in my riding concerning a number of problems. I was very careful in that survey not to weight it politically but,

rather, to weight it in the direction in which I wanted the person to think. Dealing with the unemployment situation, the results received in several instances were not those I had anticipated; but after taking a second look at them I realized that in many cases I had put something into the question which I really did not intend. It could have been misinterpreted.
One question asked whether people were paying unemployment insurance and there was a follow-up question asking whether they had ever drawn unemployment insurance benefits. I was surprised to find there were people who had paid unemployment insurance for long periods but their answers had no relationship to questions involving the operation of the unemployment insurance fund. I decided the reason for this was that the employer was also paying unemployment insurance. I did not ask that this person concern himself with answering the questionnaire and therefore I did not anticipate the result I obtained.
I believe that much of the result comes from the way in which the question is asked. In many instances the questions asked are never published with the results of the survey, so one is never really sure to what the yes or no answer pertains or what the implication is in the series of questions asked. I believe anyone who has read the results of flamboyant polls which give a great deal of credit on one side or another should seriously consider whether this is not really a form of misadvertising. I suggest it does not always work exactly in the way one would expect.
In the recent election in Ontario a number of polls indicated that the New Democratic Party was in a position to form the government. The government gave a great deal of credit to this position. It is my opinion that the poll worked in the reverse manner because obviously a number of people would have liked to take a chance on a number of New Democrats but were not willing to take a chance on the New Democratic Party forming the government of Ontario. This poll produced a violent reaction which I am sure the pollsters had not contemplated.
The point I am making is that I believe all polls are subject to interpretation. However, I believe the publishing of the results of polls has an effect on an election. It has the effect not only of conveying information but also of producing a positive result. If members do not believe there is such a positive result, then most advertisers in the same field are throwing away their money by conducting polls and publishing the results. With the long experience of some of the companies I have mentioned in this field, I do not think they would be throwing away their money in this regard.
I believe polls should be taken for the purpose of assessing how the attitudes of people are developed. I think any advertising agency which is conducting an advertising campaign, political or otherwise, should be assessing the situation and I agree entirely with the hon. member who said that the results of polls should not be published at the time of an election because they are misleading. If they are effective at all, they are effective in creating a result which has nothing to do with the orderly process upon which we embark when democratically selling the ideas of a particular candidate and a particular political party. I
April 18, 1972

hope the House will divide on this matter and will vote in favour of the motion of the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, my interest in this piece of legislation grew as I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates) when he talked of the outcome of a provincial election in Quebec, which might have been caused precisely by the publication of the results of a poll taken a few days before the election. Well, I would not like to go over this election in Quebec, which everybody remembers and took place in April 1970.
On the other hand, I would like to be specific and make clear the causes of the defeat of the Parti Quebecois which was mentioned earlier. These causes are completely foreign to the results of the poll taken during the days before the election. They have nothing to do with the figures which were reported, and, as somebody was saying very rightly, a political party which cannot overcome the results of such a poll does not deserve to be elected.
The Parti Quebecois came up with several reasons to try and justify its defeat. They even claimed that news reports had made light of the inability of those people to form a government. They also said that the electoral map was badly divided in the province of Quebec, and that this favoured some parties against their own.
They also said that the Liberal party had spent ten times as much on its election campaign as had the Parti Quebecois. I think that some joker summarized very briefly what happened in April 1970 when he said that the factor which caused the defeat of the Parti Quebecois was the fact that too many Quebecers voted Liberal.
