speakeroldname: Mr. Ambrose Hubert Peddle (Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in principle I support Bill C-170. However, I cannot support the "on again, off again" manner of the government in dealing with this legislation. Many moons ago it started out as a white paper, then it became Bill C-264 on September 13 of last year. Bill C-264, the original bill, contained the implementation date of May 1 of this year. I do not see any good reason why the original bill could not have been passed last September and any weaknesses in it or any amendments to it considered at a later date. But no, the government repeatedly refused to bring the bill before us for debate. The House will remember that they allowed it to die on the order paper. Now they have finally brought it back in the form of Bill C-170.
This bill contains no suggestion as to when it might be implemented. It comes back to us as an open-ended package which this "just society" government, this "friend of the poor" government will use as and when it sees fit as part of its noticeably accelerating process of voter manipulation.
Sir, allowing the original Bill C-264 to die on the order paper without being brought forward for debate, despite the pleas of the opposition, represents a new low in what I would call political cowardice, and with a fair degree of conniving too. First, this government became noted for its policy of governing by white paper. We all remember the deluge of white papers that was being spewed forth. Public opinion had to be tested on everything. You would almost swear it was a minority government, because it trod so gingerly, instead of a government that had been given a mammoth mandate in 1968. It had been given a large majority and I contend it was given that majority to govern.
We on this side of the House on many occasions have criticized the government for its cowardly reluctance to use the mandate that was given to it by the people, a mandate to govern by legislation and not by white paper. Somehow, members of the government appear to have taken our advice. But now they have sunk to a new low, not only with this bill but with others such as the competition bill. The government has tended to introduce legislation and then wait for reaction from the people and from the provincial governments. If the reaction is not completely favourable, the government in effect withdraws the legislation, as in the case of the original bill, by allowing it to die on the order paper. It is what is known as chickening-out.
What this country needs is a government with ability and courage. I think this government is lacking in the former and is almost completely devoid of the latter. There comes a point when any self-respecting government, out of common decency alone must realize that it can go only so far in using the people's own money in an attempt to manipulate their political support. I contend that there comes a point when this process becomes obscene, and I think that point has been reached in this particular case.

April 18, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
I wish to make a few specific remarks on a few points in the bill that strike me as making little sense. I have only to take my own riding of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador to indicate what I mean. There is a stipulated figure at which a family is cut off from receiving any family allowance under the new proposal. Let us take the case of a family in the city of Montreal that has an income of $8,000 a year. For argument's sake, let us say that in that family there are six children, three below the age of 12 and three above the age of 12 but under 17. According to this bill, that family will receive a total family allowance cheque of $85 a month.
Let us take the case of a similar family in Labrador City, Wabush or Goose Bay in my riding. The family has six children, three below the age of 12 and three above the age of 12 but under 17. Let us say that family has an income of $10,000 a year. Compared with the family in Montreal which will receive $85 a month, the family in Labrador City will receive a family allowance cheque of $45 a month. There is a difference in the salaries of the two families, $8,000 in Montreal and $10,000 in Labrador City, but an agency of the government, the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, on the basis of its studies agrees that $8,000 in Montreal is equal to the $10,000 income in Labrador City. Yet under the proposed new family allowance scheme the government will pay some $500 less per year to the family in Labrador City.
I contend that the DBS only skimmed the surface in dealing with the differential in the cost of living as between Labrador City and Montreal. In addition to everything else, winters in Labrador City are longer and as a result fuel costs are higher. It costs more to clothe and feed children in Labrador City. I repeat that the government's own agency agrees that $8,000 in Montreal is equal to $10,000 in Labrador City, yet the government says it will pay the family in Labrador City $500 a year less in family allowances than it will pay to the family in Montreal. Surely justice and common sense would dictate that this differential, when it is recognized by an agency of the government, ought to be recognized in the implementation of this bill.
There is another point that should be made. While I agree with the basic theory of the bill, in my opinion the scheme should be based on the income of the principal wage earner of the family. However imperfect the tax reform legislation which we passed, it contains measures to compensate working wives for day-care costs in respect of their children. The new Unemployment Insurance Act provides for maternity benefits to be paid to pregnant women while they are away from work to have their children. In contrast to this positive step, the family income security plan takes a negative step and actually penalizes working wives through its cut-off level which is based on gross family income rather than the income of the principal wage earner.
If a wife goes out to work to supplement the meagre salary of her husband, under the new proposal it is likely that the addition of her income will push the total family income above the cut-off level and she will therefore forfeit part or all of the family allowance. For a middle-class wife this may not be too important, but for families
(Mr. Peddle.]
struggling to get out of poverty even the loss of the family allowance cheque will hurt. The family income security plan is a disincentive for working mothers who know that they will lose part or all of their allowance as a result of their initiative.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Cut-off levels should be based not on income after deductions but, rather, on gross income. In this way personal income tax exemptions and child-care deductions would have full power for working mothers. Cut-off levels could then be scaled to ensure that the less advantaged families benefit most from the family allowance. Speaking of cut-off levels, Mr. Speaker, you do not have to be an expert to observe the inconsistency of many government departments in their assessment of when families need government support. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) took into account the fact that it costs more to raise a child when he reaches the age of 12. I appreciate the wisdom of that. However, in the new Income Tax Act the former minister of finance did not recognize the fact that children are more expensive to raise, until they reach the age of 16.
There is here a breakdown in logic and communication. According to Bill C-170, the Minister of National Health and Welfare believes that a family with one child and a gross income of $4,500 a year or less should receive maximum assistance from his department, while the Department of Finance continues to impose a substantial tax on the same person. I think this points out the serious inconsistency of the government's views.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Lack of communication.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: As I said at the outset, basically I agree with the proposal in Bill C-170, but I am going to make a very serious suggestion and I am pleased that the minister is in the House. I have had some unkind things to say about what I believe was the motivation for delaying this bill, but perhaps I have been too harsh. Perhaps I have been wrong.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: No, no.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
I will be the first to admit it if I am wrong. However, I suggest to the minister and to the government that they prove to the people of Canada that they have acted in good faith. Bill C-264 was read the first time on September 13, 1971, and the government promised that the new legislation would come into effect on May 1, 1972, just a few days from now. Let the government prove their good faith by making these payments due to the people who qualify under this program retroactive to May 1, 1972, no matter how long it will take to pass the legislation. I make that suggestion very seriously, Mr. Speaker. I know there will be objections to it. Government members will say, "What about the people who do not benefit? Will they be asked to pay it back?" But that is the government's problem and they have to live with it.
As in so many other cases, this government has raised the hopes of a large number of Canadian people. The minister said that some two million families would benefit and he promised that this legislation would be in effect on
April 18, 1972

May 1 this year. I am calling upon the government now to make that promise good, no matter how long it takes to get the bill through the remainder of the legislative process, and to make the payments retroactive to May 1, 1972.
I think the government has vacillated on this program. It started out in May, 1970, with a white paper which was not acceptable: it came back on September 13, 1971, in the form of Bill C-264. Despite the pleas of the opposition, even in that extraordinary session of parliament I believe I am correct in saying that our party pleaded that the House stay and deal with it, but the government obviously did not want it passed. I do not now want to hear any suggestion that the government does not go along with this reasonable proposal that they should prove their good faith, nor do I want to hear any suggestion that the original bill was held up because of obstruction by the opposition. Such is not the fact. I maintain that the government had ulterior motives for holding back this legislation, and I call upon them to prove their good faith and make me a liar by implementing this bill as fast as possible and by making the payments to those who would benefit effective May 1 this year.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this all-important piece of legislation because of its historical basis in the Canadian social system. We in Canada have seen great progress made in the development of our system of social security, a system which is a basic right of Canadians. One need only recall the nineteenth century and its barbaric lack of laws for protecting the ordinary citizen, and compare that century with our society today, to recognize some of the fundamental changes that have been made. These changes did not come easily; some of them were fought hard for. The history of the development of our social security system goes back to 1926 when the Liberal government of the day was forced to introduce old age pensions across the board, mainly because of the pressure of a small minority in this House which forced the government to bring in such legislation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: They did it to save their necks.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
At the time there was talk of governments not being able to afford this type of program. I did not hear this, of course, but the debates are recorded. It was argued that this would be too great an expense, that people had no right to such pensions, and so on. Now, Mr. Speaker, the old age pension is paid and it has been increased, although by minimal amounts.
In the developments that have led up to the family income security plan there have been other developments which have recognized the social rights of Canadians as members of productive units. These developments have helped in the productivity of the work force of the Canadian nation. After the Second World War, family allowances were paid to all Canadians with families, regardless of religion, race, creed or colour. The family allowance was paid as of right, as a commitment of the community to the youth of the nation. It was paid because we were committed to the idea of developing a society in which people could live with dignity and justice. The
Family Income Security Plan
family allowance cheque was particularly significant in my family. I recall how important that cheque was for my mother. It helped her to take care of her children, to provide them with basic necessities as well as provide a little spending money.
Mr. Speaker, it may be said that the family allowance program was a move that enabled women to reach a certain plateau of equal rights in our society. The allowance enabled them to exercise responsibility in financial matters connected with the family. In the neighbourhood in which I grew up, I recall that family allowances meant a great deal to mothers no matter what was the basic income of the family. The cheque was important because it helped in the raising of children and maintaining the well-being of the family structure, because by using that allowance month after month the family taught the child the responsibility of handling money and spending it. I think that was important, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps members of cabinet who deal with major issues may not be very impressed with this argument and may not think it too important, yet it is important in our society because the allowance represents a protection, a social right enjoyed by all Canadian families.
The government has introduced its family income security plan. The name of the program sounds impressive. In the last few years I have learned that whatever legislation this government introduces, the name of the legislation is always impressive. It may be a grain income stabilization bill, an income supplement program for old age pensioners or, as now, the family income security plan. This legislation is based on the principle of selectivity, on the principle of reintroducing the means test as a means of checking on family income. It is not based on any concept of social right in our society. It is based on dividing our society into those who have and those who have not. It is based on an assumption that I call piecemeal Robin Hood-ism on the part of the Liberal government.
Piecemeal Robin Hood-ism may be defined as an attempt to take from the rich to give to the poor. It is like the wife of Louis XVI telling the people to eat cake. It has nothing to do with the productivity of our society and everyone's right to share in it. It is not based on any concept of social right. It is merely a piecemeal program under which the government, following the advice of its bureaucrats and technocrats, is out to sabotage the social security system of the Dominion of Canada. Of course, in the long run, this program will be dropped. This is the first step in that direction. In the meantime, the government wants to cushion the effect of removing the family allowance altogether and a selected group within our society is to remain sheltered.
It is important to consider what the government is doing by adhering to the principle of selectivity. In the neighbourhood in which I grew up, all families were paid the family allowance regardless of family income. The family that lived down the street got the allowance, just as did our family, and our positions were comparable. Under this proposal, the family down the street might get a cheque but my family might not. Clearly, this scheme will create stigmas within our society. It will become a method

April 18, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
by which the local grocery store will note your low income by the size of your cheque.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we are concerned not only with the means test, for the size of your family allowance cheque will tell everyone that you belong to a low income family. I might say that I am used to that. The amount of the cheque sent to your house will be directly related to the size of your income. It will let people know how much you earn and in that way will be as demeaning as the welfare cheque. Because it adheres to the principle of selectivity, the government will, in neighbourhoods like the one in which I grew up, create among those who receive family allowance cheques the sort of stigma that is attached to any welfare scheme.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: The hon. member is talking about discrimination and how terrible it is. Is he for it or against it?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: I hear the comments of the Tory member. His party claims to represent the small people. I remember what members of that party said in the income tax debate. No doubt we will hear from them in this debate. I remember the speeches Tory members have made on the labour code legislation. We shall see what that party does with the legislation before us.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: The hon. member should return to his written text and not ad lib.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Perhaps we shall also hear from the hon. member later. Mr. Speaker, one cannot overemphasize the basic importance of universality. The principle cannot be ignored. I should like, for a moment, to go beyond the principles involved in this legislation and talk about the principles of the plan itself, for one can see why this government disagrees with the party I represent on matters of principle.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: What principle?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
There are so many differences of principle between us that I could spend the rest of the evening discussing them with the hon. member. I think the details of the plan are well worth examining. If you look at the details, you will find an even more incredible suggestion than the selectivity principle contained in the plan. A payment of $15 a month will be made for a child up to 11 years of age and $20 a month for a child between the age of 12 and 17. An income floor of $4,500 for a family with one child is stipulated. After that, $500 a year is allowed for each additional child in the family. Families with incomes above floor level will receive smaller amounts. With each $100 of income, the benefit decreases by 33 cents.
Let us consider what may well take place. A family with one child under 12 years of age, with a family income of up to $4,500, will receive $20. A family with an income of $6,000 will receive $15.05; $7,000, $11.75; $8,000, $8.45; $9,000, $5.15; and $10,000, $1.85, but it is not payable.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
That is the Liberal just society.
[Mr. Knight.)

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
I quite agree with the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). The figures I have quoted are the benefits received by a family with one child between the 12 and 17 years of age. I earlier stated that it was for a child under 12 years of age.
A family with two children under 12 years of age, with an income of $5,000, will receive a payment of $30; $6,000, $23.40; $7,000, $16.80; $8,000, $10.20; and $9,000, $3.60. A family with five children under 12 years of age, with an income of up to $6,500, will receive $75; $7,000, $66.75; $8,000, $50.25; $9,000, $33.75; $10,000, $17.25; and $11,000, 75 cents. Even that kind of framework will develop a number of weaknesses in the plan. It will take a Philadelphia lawyer, assisted by a number of lawyers such as the minister in charge of the Wheat Board to figure this out and explain it to the people of Assiniboia and the rest of Canada. I warn members of parliament and those who run for office here that they will have to work 24 hours a day for three, six or eight weeks to try and figure out this kind of program for people in their constituencies. I can see all kinds of problems arising strictly on the basis of the detail of the plan and the selectivity principle involved.
I wish to deal with a number of weaknesses in this plan such as applications and the responsibility of the people of Canada. If a person wants to be a beneficiary under this program he must apply, complete all the reports, do the filing, inform the government of changes of income year by year, give the age of the children and inform the government each time the size of the family changes. They must file in order to receive the benefit in the first place, and inform the government of any change of income in the family. For example, if the wife goes to work, this increases the income. If a man loses his job, it reduces the income. If there are two children, which is the size of the average family in Canada, each time their ages change the government must be informed.
What is the government's reasoning behind this? Do they want to get to the point of totally discrediting any kind of social security plan in Canada? Of families receiving partial benefits, 42 per cent will receive less than at present. The question of selectivity permeates this entire plan. It causes untold problems and burdens for the Canadian people. I want to cite three examples of what could happen under this plan as it now stands. A family with one child, living in Toronto or Vancouver with an income of $5,001, will no longer receive the baby bonus. According to the government, this family is rich. A family with two children under the age of ten years, living in Toronto with an income of $9,000, will receive $3.60 per month rather than the present $12 per month. If their income increases by $1, they will be cut off. Talk about the just society, Mr. Speaker! Let me give a third example. A family living in Toronto, with five children under 12 years of age, will receive 75 cents a month if their income is $11,000. If their income is higher, they will not receive anything. An incredible mess is created by this kind of program based on selectivity.
There are other matters that ought to be looked into. I am pleased to see that the rates announced by the minister can be changed. Let us look at those rates in terms of their face value. Based on the Canada standard health
April 18, 1972

rules, the minimum expenses per child under 12 years of age, per month, are as follows: food, skim milk, 24 ounces per day, $20.50; protein, four ounces, hamburger and either two eggs or two ounces of cheese, $8.40; vegetables, carrots and waxed beans, $5; bread and margarine, whole wheat, four slices daily, $3; orange and other vitamin C juices, $3; soap and toothpaste, $1. This totals $27.90. Shelter, on the average, $15; clothing, $7.75; dentist, minimum care, $2.50. That causes one to chuckle. The monthly total is $53.16. These are outlined in the Canada standard health rules as minimum expenses per child under 12 years of age.
The government has introduced a selective program that both initially and in the long run will hurt those in the middle income bracket, people earning between $5,000 and $9,000 per year. Therefore, let us look at what the position will be when this piece of legislation is implemented. Let us look at some of the administrative jungle out of which the Canadian people will have to crawl or even shoot their way.
This legislation may very well have been introduced in an attempt to tackle Canada's unemployment problem. With unemployment running at around 6 per cent of the labour force, the government has decided to double the number of people employed in administering the program compared with the number who administer the present family allowance program. Where the government now employs some 730 people, under this program, according to an answer placed in Hansard on December 27, 1971, the number employed will rise to 1,477.1 am willing to predict today that even if this program is implemented by next fall many, many more people will be required to figure out some of the problems created as a result of the selective nature of the program.
The cost to the department of this program alone will be about $13.7 million. This does not include court costs, the cost of the tax appeal board and other government agencies. These costs will mount because the government will ever be searching for those who do not properly fill in their applications for income security. There is one interesting sidelight to this, and it is that in order to get the plan before the public the government will have to undertake a massive advertising campaign from one end of the country to the other. Who will benefit from that? One has only to think of those who show up at Liberal party dinners in Toronto to suspect who will benefit.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Simpsons and Eatons.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Yes, but I do not think they will handle the advertising. That will be a job for Maclaren and Foster. If the government wants competely to botch up the program, they will turn over the advertising campaign to Information Canada. The only good that will come out of this selective program will be the benefits received by friends of the government, friends who are becoming fewer by the day.
There are seven distinct sets of circumstances in which applications under the plan must be filled out. First of all, one has to make an application. Then you must reapply if your income goes either up or down, if the number of
Family Income Security Plan
your children changes, if there is a change in the age of the children, and so on. This is going to keep people employed continually in the department and I would suggest such complexity will not meet the needs of the Canadian people as a whole.
With this plan, the government is creating an immense bureaucratic and administrative jungle. Those of us who spent the Christmas recess in our ridings know that many people came to our doors to see us about the difficulties they have experienced under the Unemployment Insurance Act, with all the different matters within the act, all the exceptions to the rule, all the difficulties with the cards that the computer would not accept or would not send out. All winter we have handled case after case dealing with claims for unemployment insurance because the government has listened to technocrats and bureaucrats and decided that it had a nice little plan which it could apply selectively and with which the new computer would be able to deal.
As it turned out, Mr. Speaker, the computer was not able to deal with the plan and as a result claimants went for months without payment. Next fall I suspect we will see the same kind of process going on, except that every family in Canada will in one way or another become involved with the problems of this plan.
I should like to put some other matters on the record in relation to administrative difficulties connected with this bill. All applications for family allowance must be checked to determine the eligibility of the applicant. In the case of eligible applicants, benefit payments must be calculated on the family income and age of the children. In the case of non-eligible applicants, appeals and explanations must be handled. Statements disclosing a substantial increase or decrease in income must be processed, with appropriate adjustments made to benefits. Divorces, separations and marriages must be reported if family income is affected, and benefits must be adjusted. Adjustments must be made to benefits where estimated income differs significantly from actual income. Administrative machinery must be set up to recover benefits paid out to ineligible persons. Administrative machinery must be set up to detect frauds, including misrepresentation of income, misrepresentation of the number of children, misrepresentation of the age of children, failure to report income increases, failure to report deaths, marriages, and so on. Administrative machinery for liaison with the provinces will have to be established.
All this means an incredible jungle. I am sure that if the hon. member for Essex (Mr. Whelan) viewed this plan with a great deal of seriousness he would join the opposition's stand on this bill and repeat what he said about co-ops and credit unions. Then if this bill still went through, he would resign. I appeal to the commonsense of government members. I appeal to their reason; therefore, I may well fail in my appeal. But I want to tell the House that in view of the selective basis of this bill it will go down as a regressive step that has been taken in an important social welfare program in Canada.
Let me deal with the whole question of income as it is referred to in the bill. I wish to ask a number of questions

April 18, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
which I hope the minister will answer. While travelling in my riding during the Easter recess a number of people drew my attention to their difficulties and concern about whether this plan is based on gross income. They were concerned about how it will affect the family farm. If we look at page 6 of Bill C-170, we find that the benefit will be $20 minus 33 cents for each full $100 of income by which the income of the child's family for the base calendar year exceeds $4,500 when the child is the only child in the family, or the aggregate of $4,500 and the amount obtained by multiplying the number of children in that family in excess of one by $500 when that child is not the only child in the family.
In each place reference is made to income without any description as to whether it is taxable, net or gross income. This is an important matter which ought to be explained very clearly during all stages of this bill, because it makes a great deal of difference to every farmer and small businessman in Canada in terms of income definition. Let me refer to page 2 of the bill, clause 2(2)(a) which states that the income of a person for a calendar year is his income for that year computed in accordance with the provisions of the Income Tax Act applicable thereto. The clause goes on to provide that this is minus the amount of any death benefit paid to the taxpayer in that year under the Canada Pension Plan or any provincial pension plan as defined in the act. That part of the bill again refers to the Income Tax Act. I quote that paragraph of clause 2 as follows:
(a) the income of a person for a calendar year is his income for that year computed in accordance with the provisions of the Income Tax Act applicable thereto, minus the amount of any death benefit paid to him in that year under the Canada Pension Plan or a provincial pension plan as defined in that Act-
There is reference to the so-called income tax bill, that piece of reform passed last year which will long be remembered for its non-reform. Let us look at this matter in terms of the definition of income. On page 2 in division B, under computation of income we find that the income of a taxpayer for a taxation year for the purpose of this bill is his income for the year determined by the following rules, and then it goes on to provide that you must determine the aggregate of amounts each of which is the taxpayer's income for the year, other than a taxable capital gain from the disposition of a property, from a source inside or outside Canada, including, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, his income for the year from each office, employment, business and property.
If we turn to page 26 of that reform bill we find the following provision in paragraph (g):
any amount received by the taxpayer in the year that was dependent upon the use of or production from property whether or not that amount was an instalment of the sale price of the property (except that an instalment of the sale price of agricultural land is not included by virtue of this paragraph)-
That is a further reference to definition of income. I see that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray) is in the House. Perhaps he will take the opportunity to explain to the House in some detail the effect of the family income security plan in terms of whether it is based on over-all, net or gross income or taxable income.
We are faced with another difficulty because of the selectivity of this program and its over-all commitment to 
dividing Canadians into haves and have-nots. There are other aspects of this plan which make it obvious that someone in the government is not up to par. When I look at the plan and realize it is based on income, knowing that the income of people changes from year to year, I begin to wonder whether the government took a member of the task force on agriculture and put him with the group which drafted this income security plan. We have here the creation of selectivity in respect of a group of people, particularly the farmers in the west whose incomes are based on international markets over which they have no control, a transportation system over which they have little or no control, and prices over which they have no control.
The government is now telling these people that under the income security plan they must adjust their incomes for each year that it changes. A farmer's income can change from one year to the next by thousands of dollars, as can the income of a fisherman or a small businessman. I am not sure that this applies to the legal profession.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Take it from me, it can.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
My colleague suggests that it can. What I am trying to get at is that there is great complexity in this legislation as a result of a simple matter of selectivity. The government sits idly back and will go to the people during the next federal election and tell them what it is doing for the poor. I suggest all the government is doing is erecting flagpoles in front of their homes and flying flags.
There is one thing about Liberalism in respect of legislation, and anyone who studies history will know this. It is that Liberalism is based on the philosophy of changing things a little bit here when it is too late, and a little bit there when it is too late. Liberals bring in certain kinds of social reform but they never get to the heart of the matter. They never tackle the problems of the minorities in our society and they never tackle the corporate industries in terms of proper taxation. They continue to protect the economic system from any kind of change that might benefit the Canadian people.
This program is intended to be based on a guaranteed income. It should be based on a net income for every citizen, rather than on a type of selectivity which lumps people in the position of haves and have-nots in comparison with that group in our society which has a great deal.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say a few words on Bill C-170. First of all, I must say that I am completely in favour of an increase of family allowances, as I have been for a long time. In fact, I have always wondered, each year, why successive governments did not increase the amount of those allowances or ever ventured to bring them into line with the cost of living.
We have seen all other pensions periodically increaded while governments never stopped to try to adjust these allowances, leaving them still at the same rate.
Today, an increase is being proposed. First we are told that they will be increased to $15 for children under 12 and to $20 for children aged 16 and 17. Upon reading the
April 18, 1972

bill, it is clear that we are losing the very essence of these allowances, their universality. We will again be having selective allowances, to which I am opposed. It is enough that old age pensions be awarded on that basis, which is more costly than granting a $55 pension to all old people.
I believe that if we make the same mistake for family allowances there will be no end to payment of investigators throughout Canada. I suggest that it will cost the government more to finance all this bureaucracy, investigating about each child, in each family, each month about the parents salaries in order to check whether a child is getting the proper amount.
I wonder whether that is not one of the government's devices for creating employment. That is also what I figured when the guaranteed income for old people was brought forward. Everyone is taxed to give all old people $50, but it is evident that only about 40 per cent of the elderly get $55. However, it costs more in salaries to withhold this supplementary income from some 50 percent of the elderly. It would save the government money just to pay out the pension to all old people, even those who do not need it. At the end of the year they would just return it by way of taxes.
We shall have the same situation for family allowances. As in the case of old people, there will be discrimination applied to children.
That selective system which takes away from some people to give to others reminds me of a nursery of 50 children where milk would be taken from the bottle of the fatter baby and given to the leaner one. The measure is as ridiculous as that!
The child, if considered as a human being, is entitled, as a member of society, to social justice. If I want to be fair to ten children, I will not see them as coming from poor or rich families, but as human beings. And if the state wants to exercise justice and grant them an equitable social allowance, it should give to each of them the same amount.
Being rich or poor is the father's problem and not that of the child. As concerns social justice, it applies to the child. If some father is richer, let us forget about it because at the end of the year, the state will catch up with him through his income tax return. Let's not worry. First of all, let us be fair to the child, let us consider him as a full-fledged human being entitled to receive justice personally.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that if the universality factor of family allowances is abolished, this will destroy an undertaking that started several years ago. Since its inception, the present system has applied across the board. Without any consideration being given to the family income, the children under 10 receive $6 per month, and those 10 and over up to 16 receive $8 per month.
In the province of Quebec, the provincial government pays an additional $10 a month for children from 16 to 17 years of age inclusively who attend school. The province gets this amount back from the federal government. Again in the province of Quebec, the government also pays, in bi-yearly payments, the following amounts per year: for the first child, $30; for the second, $35; for the third, $40; for the fifth, $50; and for the sixth, $70. You
Family Income Security Plan
have to add to those amounts $10 a year for each child from 10 to 16 years of age.
Mr. Speaker, it can be said of family allowances paid in the province of Quebec at present that they are universal, since they are paid for all children, whereas the new legislation provides for a selective method.
I think that many problems will arise in the calculation of allowances to be paid for those children. Moreover, the great number of bureaucrats needed may cost more than would the payment of $15 for each and every child. Besides, we will have to make sure that some family heads pay this amount back to the treasury, as is done at present. At the present time, family allowances are universal, and at the end of the year we pay back in income tax any overpayment received, but at least the child has the comfort of being able to say: I get my allowance. Once again this is the problem of the family head.
In this legislation, as is stipulated in subparagraphs (a), (b), and (c) of clause 6(1), there is a ceiling on family income, and whenever the family income exceeds this ceiling, allowances paid in respect of children are reduced, or sometimes abolished, depending on circumstances. According to the bill under consideration, the amounts of benefits ranging from $15 to $20 will be reduced to 33 cents per each $100 of income. As I said a while ago, it is interesting to examine a table of income to determine what a child will receive in relation to his parents' wages.
I have done some quick figuring in this connection. For example, if a family with one child earns $6,000, from that income will be deducted the maximum income of the mother and father which will make a difference of $1,500, that is a reduced benefit of $4.95. The child will therefore draw an allowance of $15 less $4.95, that is $10.05. If the parents have two children, the maximum amount is $4,500 plus $500, that is $5,000. The total amount of $6,000 less $5,000 gives $1,000 or 10 times a reduction of 33 cents that is $3.30. The child will therefore get $11.70.
In a family with four children, still drawing a $6,000 income, the child will get-I did not figure it out, but in any event it is easy to do so.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: It is hard to figure out!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
It may be and it will be even more complicated in a little while.
In the case of a couple who earn $8,000, Mr. Speaker, and have one child the ceiling is $4,500; the allowance is $11.55. When there are two children, if the total salary is $10,000, the ceiling is $5,500 and the benefit is reduced by $18.15. We then realize what the situation is; then the act tells us that when the payment is less than $5, the child gets nothing, not even 15 cents per month.
This of course will be based on the revised salary of the father and mother, the salary made in the last year. If on the other hand the father's salary increases or decreases during the years, of course new inquiries and new calculations will be required to find out what each child will get. In Quebec, there are even families with ten children.

April 18, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
Imagine the calculations and the bureaucracy that will be required solely to control selective family allowances. One would think that the government is looking for Chinese puzzles. I really don't know whether the government is trying to create jobs or increase their number but by multiplying them it is also multiplying the headaches for everyone. It is also multiplying administrative costs, and the injustices towards every Canadian citizen. Without fail, all those inquiries will lead to injustices as is the case year in and year out with the old people.
If only we could have impartial and infallible inspectors. But that is impossible. They are human. We always tend to protect those we love more or punish a little those we love less, and then the tug of war starts. There lies the work of the member of a riding. If only selectivity did not exist, the member would have 50 per cent fewer problems or cases to solve. We should try to connect this with the inspector who has not done his duty, or has not done it properly, or perhaps has done it too well in some instances.
This whole issue stems here again, from those selective allowances that are provided for in this bill. When it was before the committee, I had a chance to read the briefs that were submitted, and I kept thinking: this government will certainly be under pressure and will agree with the recommendations contained in these briefs to the effect that in 80 per cent of cases, people feel that the government should make the allowances universal. That is why I am surprised, after having read so many briefs opposing this bill, that this government has stuck to its guns.
We are then going to keep on with our speeches for perhaps a day or two, but we will necessarily have to vote, and I am sure that this will not change anything in the bill. This bill was drafted by departmental officials who, I fear, do not know how to erase once in a while. They will not change anything in the bill. They stick to selectivity, and this we cannot accept. To give another idea of the protests, I can say that I have received 50 more letters. I wish to quote a few newspaper articles. The minister has probably read what they have to say about this selectivity. I quote:
Strong opposition to the exclusion of 40 per cent of families from family allowances.
Taking for granted that the child is a contribution to society much more than to the family, Les Organismes Familiaux Associes du Quebec objected, in a statement of position published yesterday, to the elimination of 40 per cent of families from the family allowance plans as proposed respectively by the governments of Quebec and Ottawa.
Through this statement, this group which represents tens of thousands of families in the province places so to speak the debate on this question in its true perspective, namely, the responsibility of the state to assume with the parents the financial burden of bringing up children tomorrow's adults.
We must keep in mind that in Quebec two families out of five will be cut off next May 1st from the family allowances because of the selective approach adopted by both government levels; eligibility will be based on family income and on the number of children.
Now, the family organizations do feel that this cutting off will mean "losing a right gained 25 years ago."
Those remarks were published in the newspaper Le Soleil on January 6, 1972. May I quote from another source which is not the least important one: the farmers' wives of the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean area who met to

protest against this bill, against the selective feature of this bill. They are not against the principle of the bill, for they approve of the increase, but they also advocate the universality of the allowances. This is the reason why the AFEAS, formerly known as the farmers' wives groups, will hold their convention in Jonquieres on May 16. There was a preliminary meeting and I would like to quote from the report of that meeting. Here it is:
During the past three months, the women of the Urban Committee of the AFEAS have asked the advice of many members in order to learn their views on the family allowances system.
Most of the women questioned have stated that they did not approve the programs as introduced by the provincial and federal governments. They said that the allowance was withdrawn at a time where a child needed it most that is when he was undertaking higher studies. The women also suggested that an allowance should be granted from five years of age and raised according to the age of the child and the cost of living, because they said that their financial problems increased when the young people were entering high school.
The following was stated about a report on universality:
A report submitted by the responsible members of the Urban Committee points out that the women questioned were in favour of an universal and taxable allowance on the entire family income. This formula, according to the report, would be the fairest way of giving to those who have little money and to take from those who have too much.
The report adds that selectivity as applied to family allowances is a step more reminiscent of social welfare than of children's aid.
The women consulted also opposed the way the government intended to increase the allowances after the fourth child if those 18 or over are excluded. When they reach that age, allowances will no longer be paid for them, although more money is needed for them for clothing, food, school fees and recreation costs, the report goes on to say.
On the subject of the responsibility incumbent on governments, it adds:
Our governments have some responsibility toward the family. Parents do not bring up children for their own sake but for that of society. The betterment of family life should prevail over political advantage. So, those women believed that the above-mentioned legislation promoted a higher birth-rate among the people not so well off and a sharper fall in the birth-rate among those in the middle income bracket.
Moreover, those women are asking that a survey be conducted among students aged 18 years or more on their financial assistance. The report suggests that this is inconsistent with the tax allowance for dependents. Those women also point out that governments will have to take income into account in connection with the poverty line.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted the House to be aware of this evidence. Surely the committee has heard quite a few of these representations but we can see that they have changed nothing. We still stand where we stood the day the bill was introduced and I am convinced that this situation will continue. We are going to debate and vote and nobody will dare criticize the government and force it to re-introduce the old family allowances formula and universality even though 80 per cent of the population is asking for it.
Once more, I wonder why the government is repeatedly bringing forward this selectivity concept which nobody wants. This is why I again urge the House to think it over before passing this legislation. As for those still in a position to influence the government, let them speak reason to it and let it be known that universality of family allowances is requested by most of our citizens.
April 18, 1972

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like, in turn, to make some comments on this bill which is definitely deemed to be one of the most important pieces of legislation this Parliament should pass in the near future.
Of course, Bill C-170, providing for an increase of family allowances is accepted in principle by all members of this House and I think that the Canadian people look favourably upon the increase of these allowances.
Surely, it is not sufficient to merely criticize the government for the provisions of this bill. I think it is important to note that the tabling of this legislation has required a considerable period of time while we are well aware that thousands of households have long been awaiting an increase compatible with the cost of bringing up a child.
There is a so-called selectivity principle, but others favour universality. I think that there is a difference of opinion in this respect. It is my understanding that by tabling this legislation, the government has sought to increase the benefits for those who need them most and naturally to reduce those received by household heads who can easily provide for the upkeep of their children.
I listened to several speeches, and I have to respect the opinion of each and everyone. Personally, however, I would be tempted to favour selectivity, unlike others who maintain that the same allowance should be paid all over the country, and for every child.
I think it is a mistake to give too much importance to the payment being made to the child. In all fairness, we should, according to some members, give every child the same allowance. Certainly as far as this goes, this is valid reasoning, but we know very well that in practice it is not really the child who spends the money. The child certainly has a part in his parents' expenses, but we know very well that family allowances are in fact spent or administered by the family head.
I feel that under a selective plan, a low-income family will be able to receive an appreciable, if not sufficient, increase. From there, I think there was an attempt-and this is the way in which I understand this legislation-to narrow the gap between the big man and the little man, as they are commonly called.
For instance, a few years ago, we granted a national across the board salary increase of 6 per cent. On this basis, people said that in a just society you had to grant a 6 per cent increase to all, which, in my opinion, was extremely unfair, since the man who made $3,000 could only receive a $180 increase, while the man who made $20,000 got a $1,000 increase. I think that this widened the gap between the big man and the little man even further.
Now the proposed selective scheme leads me to think that we are heading for a readjustment in favour of the really under privileged family, at least the family that needs it most.
I surely deplore the fact that a number of families will have to do without family allowances.
When members of a "cercle de fermieres", for instance-a group of people who are not considered as high-salaried people-are against a selective program, I am surprised, because the farmers, considering their
Family Income Security Plan
income, will surely not be at a disadvantage on account of a bill like this one. I rather believe that from $10,000 up, a number of families will have to do without their allowances.
We also know that two families out of five, in the province of Quebec, will lose their family allowances. However, we know full well that three out of five families need it that much more. To my mind, it is really a matter of redistribution amongst the most needy and I sincerely think that we are steadily progressing towards a just society by creating a more acceptable social climate.
I am tempted to support this bill because I believe in selectivity. We should have redistributed those allowances amongst the neediest a long time ago.
I am sorry that 40 per cent of all Canadian families will have to do without family allowances. On the other hand, I feel that the other 60 per cent will derive greater benefit, and they are the ones who need it most.
I am quite convinced that selectivity is better than universality. I think it is appropriate and I for one want to support it.
We know that the administrative costs of such a program will increase. To say that the complexity of these formulas would incite us to refrain from any action is a negative attitude. I realize that this will not be easy, that it will be complicated, but despite the complications we had with the new unemployment insurance benefits, I know also that Canadians were generally in favour of increasing these benefits.
I hope that the experience we had with unemployment insurance will benefit Parliament and that the government will be prepared to apply this formula. And I also think that such an experience will prompt it to make further preparation.
The minister has quoted a while ago figures about the administration costs, which are quite different from those given tonight, suggesting that the increased family allowance would be less than the additional administration costs.
I think the hon. members should not listen to such arguments. But then again, between doing nothing and doing something, even if it entails some difficulties, there is a difference. I know that any new formula raises problems, but I wanted to be positive. I recognize that there are difficulties and I urge the government to eliminate them as soon as possible.
It is understandable that the administration costs will be higher than they are now, due to an important change. But we must also consider the advantages and recognize them.
Nevertheless, I would remind the minister involved to review calculations. I admit that they are highly controversial. For those whose income is under $10,000 a year, taking into account a certain number of children, I believe it would be equitable to review the calculations. In fact, it must be recognized that for an average-size family, an income of $10,000 cannot be considered as excessive. I also feel that, taking the cost of living into consideration, those who have an income of $15,000 can more readily stand this deduction.

April 18, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
However, while remaining very positive, I should like to ask the minister responsible to review calculations. I hope that when we reach the committee stage recommendations will be submitted. I believe agencies will appear to make representations to the minister. I dare hope he will consider reviewing his figures and making the adjustments called for. This bill certainly warrants further amendment.
I suggest that the selectivity principle is quite justifiable and acceptable, and since it will be possible to make representations in committee and it is hoped that the government will reconsider some calculations, I think that the legislation before us has a great deal of merit. I hope that it will be implemented for the benefit of low-income families. We recognize that it is urgent to help them.
Before concluding my remarks, I should like to ask the minister to give substantial assistance to 18-year-olds to enable them to complete their studies. We know that from age 18, children have greater needs, as a high percentage of them are heading for universities or other institutions of higher learning. Should we not think seriously about a scheme to help them until completion of their studies?
We have recognized that at 18, a child attains his majority, but we also know that in fact, he remains a student until he is 22, 23, 24 and sometimes 25.
In fact, I wonder whether the government should not help him financially so that he could further his studies, even under a selective plan.
This would certainly contribute to the establishment of a social climate more appropriate and more encouraging for the children, thereby easing the burden of fathers who have much difficulty making ends meet.
Mr. Speaker, I shall be satisfied with these few remarks, as I hope I shall have the opportunity of rising on third reading to repeat that, although I agree with the spirit of this bill, I dare hope that the government will modify a number of figures in respect of people earning $10,000 or less.
I should also invite the government to consider net instead of gross income because, owing to a number of factors, gross income is often misleading. Therefore, I submit that we should consider net income first. With the co-operation of course of all hon. members, while accepting their very positive comments, we should have the opportunity of adopting this bill as soon as possible for the welfare of the families in distress and of granting them the additional allowances provided for under the bill before us.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to enter this debate so that tomorrow, on behalf of my colleagues and on my own behalf, when I have completed my remarks or toward the end of my remarks I may move an amendment to the motion before the House. Since the recess for Easter, we have all had an opportunity to study this bill carefully and to appreciate the principles animating it better than we appreciated them before.
In our view, therefore, it is important to deal with the basic principles of the bill and some aspects of it, for what
[Mr. La Salle.)
the minister has done in this legislation is to pervert the idea behind the principle of family allowances. He has suggested that he is using family allowances as an antipoverty measure. This was never the purpose of family allowances when they were first introduced. That is not the philosophy behind payments of this sort. That was not the philosophy behind the idea when it was first presented in 1944-45, and it is the wrong philosophy with which to approach payments that are intended, basically, to assist families in bringing up their children with decency and security. This is not intended to be an anti-poverty measure. I shall in some detail point out tomorrow, when I come to the body of my remarks, that as an anti-poverty measure this is a shameful piece of tokenism which cannot accomplish anything in the field of poverty, either.
All those on the government side, the minister included, have naturally tried to put the best face on this bill while talking about the number of families that will be affected one way or another by it. It is always possible to say, when discussing bills like this, that 11 million families, or whatever the number will be, will receive more. When I hear that, the first question I ask myself and which I ask hon. members to ask themselves is, more than what? What the minister tries to get us excited about is that we will no longer pay $6 a month or $8 a month for helping to bring up a child. The payment, it is said, will become $15 or $20 a month, although I submit in most cases it will be $10, $11 or $9 a month. I will go into details tomorrow. At any rate, we are supposed to get excited about that kind of generosity. Well, Mr. Speaker, this bill is not generous, it is not thoughtful, it will not do the job and it is, as I have said, a perversion of the original idea.
What the minister said but was careful not to emphasize was that over one million families will not get anything under his plan. I should like the minister or anyone on the government side of the House to tell the people of Canada that there are one million rich families in this country which do not need any assistance to bring up their children in decency and security. In the minister's statement of March 24 there is a contradiction that I have not been able to figure out. I will mention it now as we approach ten o'clock. Perhaps the minister can enlighten us at some time. On page 1133 of Hansard, the left-hand column, the minister is reported as saying:
Two and a half million families will receive benefits. Nine hundred thousand families will receive maximum benefits.
On the next page, page 1134, in the left-hand column he says:
Full benefit under FISP will go to 1,249,000 families-
I do not understand why there is so much difference between those two figures. In one statement the minister said that 900,000 families will receive maximum benefit and in the other that 1,249,000 families will receive the full benefit. The difference of 300,000 families is not a small figure. The differential of one-third as between the figure given on page 1133 and the figure on page 1134 of Hansard is pretty large and important. I do not know which figure is correct.
What the minister did not emphasize, and what I want to emphasize tonight particularly and again tomorrow, is that over one million families will not get any benefit under this bill. As I said, I challenge the minister to tell me
April 18, 1972

and this House that there are one million rich families in this country.
With that, Mr. Speaker, perhaps you will permit me to call it ten o'clock.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

maintopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-ISSUANCE OF INTERPRETATION   BULLETIN CONCERNING DEDUCTIBILITY FROM TAXABLE INCOME OF MONEY PAID BY TORONTO "STAR" FOR "TELEGRAM" SUBSCRIPTION LISTS
NATIONAL REVENUE-ISSUANCE OF INTERPRETATION   BULLETIN CONCERNING DEDUCTIBILITY FROM TAXABLE INCOME OF MONEY PAID BY TORONTO "STAR" FOR "TELEGRAM" SUBSCRIPTION LISTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the last few years we have seen in Canada a growing monopoly of newspapers in our major centres. In the last few months we have seen that monopoly extended to one afternoon newspaper in the largest urban area of Canada, metropolitan Toronto. I think parliament and the people of Canada have not only the right but the duty to look carefully at the way in which that kind of monopoly has come about. It seems to me, on the basis of reports I have seen in newspapers and on the basis of the interpretation bulletin to which my questions today and the other day referred, that it is very likely that the public treasury will pay for the establishment of an afternoon newspaper monopoly in metropolitan Toronto. That is not what we ought to be doing; that is not what the government ought to be doing.
The first point that strikes me as odd is the coincidence of dates. According to reports, the deal between the Toronto Star and the Toronto Telegram was completed on September 15, 1971. It was announced publicly on September 18, 1971. On September 17, 1971, two days after the deal was completed and one day before it was publicly announced, the Department of National Revenue issued a bulletin. This clearly indicates that the Toronto Star will be able to deduct as a business expense the $10 million it paid for the subscribers list of the Toronto Telegram. That coincidence of dates is a very serious matter which I believe this Parliament ought to know about.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) used the adjective "pusillanimous". I say the minister made a less than heroic attempt to hide behind the income tax law in refusing to give information. I have not asked for information about the tax position of the Toronto Star! I am not interested in that. I am asking him to inform the House and the people of Canada about any correspondence between the Toronto Star and his department relating to information with respect to the possible application of the law.
I asked for information regarding conversations that may have been held by the minister and members of his department with anybody representing the Toronto Star, whether it is the publisher, Mr. Honderick, a member of the board of directors, the Hon. Walter Gordon or any-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
body else on behalf of the Star. That is not information relating to the Star's tax payments or tax liabilities. It is information regarding conversations and correspondence, using the word in the legal sense, by the department as to the application or possible application of laws and what might be done. It goes to the question of whether the department was requested, asked or pleaded with to issue some kind of interpretation bulletin such as was in fact issued on September 17 last.
During the course of the deal between the Toronto Star and the Toronto Telegram, I read in a newspaper report that the publisher of the Telegram believed that the money he was receiving for the subscribers list was a capital gain; it was payment for goodwill in the subscribers list. If the Department of National Revenue permits Mr. Bassett to have the $10 million as a capital gain, the public treasury will pay it both ways. If this is a capital gain to Mr. Bassett, it cannot be a business expense to the Toronto Star. If it is a business expense to the Toronto Star, it cannot be capital to Mr. Bassett. If the two work out as the newspaper report indicated, the public treasury will pay the part that the publisher of the Telegram would have had to pay if it were income, and will pay the part the Toronto Star would have had to pay if it were not able to deduct the $10 million as a business expense for the year.
What is it we are doing? All this is behaviour that facilitates the establishment of a monopoly in the largest afternoon newspaper market, and facilitates the loss of 1,200 jobs. The government would have been serving the welfare of this country a great deal better if instead of making possible these large tax concessions to powerful newspaper organizations it had used some of the public money to assist the Toronto Telegram to carry on so there would be some competition among newspapers in metropolitan Toronto and so that 1,200 Canadian jobs might have been retained. This would have been a service to this country. That is not in fact what has happened.
A month or two ago I raised in this House the question of the remission of $6 million in sales tax to Canadian Oil Sands Limited of Alberta, a subsidiary of the "poverty stricken", multi-national Sun Oil. We gave them a Christmas gift of $6 million. There is now the possibility that we are going to give a gift to a large, powerful newspaper corporation. Then we present to this House new legislation on family allowances which is meagre and shamefully inadequate. It is this kind of double standard that I object to, as well as the way the government carries on.
