maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY-PARTICIPATION WITH UNITED STATES IN STUDY ON POSSIBLE YEAR-ROUND OPERATION
ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY-PARTICIPATION WITH UNITED STATES IN STUDY ON POSSIBLE YEAR-ROUND OPERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like any maritimer I have a concern for the operations of the St. Lawrence Seaway. And like any Canadian I have a concern about how one can battle, if never successfully, the Canadian winter. Flying to Ottawa from Halifax in recent weeks, I have always watched whether the ice was clearing from the seaway and I gathered that the people operating the seaway are certainly having their problems with this winter.
A few days ago my attention was drawn to an article by Jeff Carruthers which appeared in the Ottawa Journal on March 14 last pointing up some experimentation that was proposed for the St. Lawrence Seaway system. I quote him as follows:
Originally intended to be called The Year of the Gulf, the program as now envisioned is to stretch from this year through 1976, with peak scientific activity for 18 months between late 1973 and spring of 1975.
The federal department of the environment, which is co-ordinating the project, is asking the federal treasury board for some $9 million for the project. A similar sum of money is to be obtained from existing budgets in participating government departments.
Federal officials say that it is almost assured that the project will be approved as proposed.
The question that brings us to the sauce for the goose tonight is one that I directed to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson), though I presume it could also have been directed to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis). In any event, it raises some questions as to the amount of money which should be used on such experimentation to keep the seaway open for longer periods in the year.
Parliamentarians are already familiar with the report by the Ottawa firm of D. William Carr and Associates. It is suggested by that group that the debt should be restructured so that it would cover only those expenditures necessary for providing facilities to shipping. The seaway should then be required to repay only the interest on the capital debt, not the debt itself.

The report also says that Canada should move to increase tolls since this country is paying five-sixths of the investment costs of the seaway and covering six-sevenths of the waterway's deficits. It suggests that even with the 5 per cent annual increase over the next five years-and it argues that there should be nothing of a greater nature- the debt-ridden seaway would not become self-sustaining. The report suggests that if tolls were increased by 5 per cent per year for five years, seaway revenues would be kept abreast of the expected increase in costs, but such a toll increase would be insufficient to cover interest, operating and maintenance costs and seaway deficits would continue to mount, though at a slower rate. The report also suggests that if there are no toll increases, by 1985 the debt will have gone up to $1.6 billion, or three times what it is today. These are awesome figures. They are available in the Carr report.
My purpose in speaking this evening is to ask someone to reply on behalf of the minister and to find out just how far the government proposes to go with any experimentation. Will an attempt be made to balance the increased benefits of a longer season with increased tolls? Is that sort of balance to be kept? Perhaps the situation is to be left as much out of joint as it is now.
I come from a part of the country where transportation subsidies are quite common. When looking at transportation as a whole, I have adopted the philosophy that this is something which can never really pay its way. No matter what biased statements are made in this place, I do not think transportation as a whole in Canada will ever pay its way. I do not think it should have to pay its way if it helps to keep the country together or open up new horizons. If it serves the public in this way, then that service is sufficient in itself.
When I hear remarks made about subsidies to maritime transportation, particularly those made by people from central Canada, and knowing the amount of money being funnelled into the St. Lawrence Seaway, I am reminded of that old con game where a fellow makes a great deal about throwing coins into the bowl of a beggar, so much so that people do not notice that with the other hand he is engaged in a modern version of the Brinks robbery.
In any event, I have asked the questions and I hope the ministry will answer by stating exactly what is proposed in respect of experimentation in so far as the St. Lawrence Seaway is concerned.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerard Duquet (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY-PARTICIPATION WITH UNITED STATES IN STUDY ON POSSIBLE YEAR-ROUND OPERATION
speechtext:
In replying to the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) I wish to express my appreciation for having an opportunity to put on the record the participation of Canadian officials in this very important matter.
This evening I can confirm the statement made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) to the hon. member on March 22. A request has not been received from the United States to contribute to their study concerning the subject of keeping the St. Lawrence Seaway open on a year-round basis. However, a study has been conducted for some time now by various federal officials from both within and without the Department of Transport, together
April 18, 1972

with provincial representatives, to study the technical difficulties as well as the economic and environmental implications of an extended seaway season. United States representatives have attended these meetings as observers and Canadian observers have attended United States meetings.
It is assuring to note the co-operation which exists between our two countries on these important discussions. I have noted a number of items in the hon. member's speech which I will be pleased to bring to the attention of the minister who I am sure will want to consider them seriously.

maintopic: INDUSTRY-CLOSING OF MCBEAN COLLIERY- PROVISION OF PENSIONS SIMILAR TO BENEFITS FOR DEVCO MINERS
INDUSTRY-CLOSING OF MCBEAN COLLIERY- PROVISION OF PENSIONS SIMILAR TO BENEFITS FOR DEVCO MINERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday when I asked the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) about his attitude in respect of pensions for the McBean miners in Thorburn, Nova Scotia, I was not trying to single out the minister for any partisan purposes but to take the opportunity once more to bring the issue of the problems involved in the closure of the McBean mine before this House. Had his colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), been in the House I would have questioned him also because he is the one to whom the final appeal was made by a delegation from Nova Scotia consisting of people from the United Mine Workers, the government of Nova Scotia and the miners themselves. However, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion is indirectly involved because the Devco operation is to some extent responsible for some of the administration of the McBean mine at Thorburn.
I am appealing tonight to the government, through the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, to once more consider the plight of the McBean mine and the miners and see if something constructive can be done even at this late date. I sincerely hope the government will take another look at the problem, because the need for coal exists in the area. A market is literally only a few miles away. The Nova Scotia Power Commission thermal plant can more than absorb this mine's total output. There are institutions and people in the area who need coal for heating and they are able to buy it, under the circumstances, at reduced rates. There are also institutions which depend on coal produced at the McBean mine who can ill-afford the cost of making other heating arrangements. However, this is a minor point because the skills of these miners, once they cease to be used, probably cannot be replaced if the mine is not kept in operation.
It is ironic in looking at the annual report of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources of a year ago to see the following statement which appears at page 73 under the heading "Phasing out of coal subventions":
As a result of the improved economic situation in western Canada and the alternative programs instituted for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick federal subventions have been phased out and will be discontinued in 1970-71.
How ironic! The western coal mining industry is doing well. Therefore, we will conveniently discontinue the subventions and effectively cripple the eastern coal mining industry. I find this very ironic. However, before dealing with this situation any further I should like to raise the
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
main issue I wish to discuss tonight. Assuming that this mine is in fact to be closed, what will be done to make certain that the miners affected will receive the type of retirement pension to which they are entitled? It seems to me it is self-evident that the government would not wish to promote discrimination among miners in one province in the same type of industry. It is bad enough to hear about discrimination in different parts of Canada, but here we have a situation in which the miners who are being administered through the Cape Breton Development Corporation are receiving pre-retirement pensions considerably greater than those scheduled to be given to the miners at the McBean mine.
It would seem to me, again, that the government, in order to be just in this case, must take several steps. It must do so immediately. It must undertake, in co-operation with the government of Nova Scotia, that the McBean colliery workers will receive exactly the same benefits as those received by their brethren in Cape Breton. It must immediately make an effort to see that the eligibility and age for the receipt of benefits is lowered. It must as soon as possible make the very best arrangements possible for high priority in respect of re-employment, with all necessary upgrading and on-the-job training.
This would only be pursuant to the policies undertaken by the then minister of energy, mines and resources some time ago. The former minister, on October 7 of last year, indicated that he would make every effort to assist in the endeavour to rehabilitate the remaining work force. He pointed out at that time that although there was, as he called it, a one time grant of $930,000 given to offset the financial losses incurred, as he said; "to the time when either the financial grant provided by Canada is exhausted or the work force employed at the McBean Mine has declined to the point where further operation of the mine is impractical," the intent of that original grant was to terminate the mining and assist in rehabilitating the work force. This was not completely accomplished and, therefore, he said: "I arranged for a second grant of $750,000."
Coincidentally, this grant came at a time when the Central Nova by-election was being contested approximately a year ago. It seems to me that at that time the government was full of largesse. They were going to do great things for Central Nova in general and for the McBean mine in particular. Unfortunately, we have seen little evidence of their good will since that time.
Without ending on a rancorous note, may I again appeal to the government to take another look at this important situation affecting 200 families and see what can be done, in the first instance, to maintain the working of this significant part of the Nova Scotia coal industry and, secondly, to make absolutely certain that there is no discrimination or unfairness in looking after the needs of the men if indeed their employment is forcibly terminated.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Bechard (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: INDUSTRY-CLOSING OF MCBEAN COLLIERY- PROVISION OF PENSIONS SIMILAR TO BENEFITS FOR DEVCO MINERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the minister I wish to say that the McBean mine is in no way connected with Devco. It is entirely a provincial responsibility. However, the minister would be happy to see that the hon. member's point of view is brought to the attention of the provincial government.
